The real opportunity, they say, isn't that nobody fixes engines, it's that almost nobody does it as a real, reliable business with an actual shop and same-day callbacks.
best: Someone younger who's willing to learn a genuine skilled trade and is comfortable with a business that gets noticeably slower in winter, since demand is seasonal for outdoor equipment.
truth: The presenters are upfront that this is one of the weaker "build a real business" plays on their list precisely because the labor takes real time to learn and the seasonality is a real constraint. It's framed as a good cash-flow trade, not an easy path to a scalable company.

name: Building a hyper-niche website targeting only 'water heater replacement' searches, then referring the leads to a plumber for a cut
cost: Low (website hosting; SEO tool subscription for keyword research)
what: Build a website focused exclusively on water heater replacement/repair (not general plumbing), targeting specific high-volume, low-competition keywords ('water heater replacement,' 'water heater replacement near me,' 'water heater repair'), rank it for a specific city using dedicated content pages, then either fulfill the service yourself or route the resulting leads to a plumber/contractor for a referral cut, replicable city by city.
pitch: The presenter cites a real plumber who flipped his entire business to focus only on water heater replacement after noticing it was his most profitable, under-targeted service, now making $700,000/year and ranking #1 in his town; keyword research shows 'water heater replacement' gets 112,000 monthly searches nationally at a 0/100 difficulty score, which the presenter says is the easiest single home-service keyword he's ever found.
best: Someone willing to learn basic SEO/keyword research and either perform the service themselves or build referral relationships with local plumbers.
truth: The cited search-volume and keyword-difficulty figures come from a named third-party SEO tool (Ahrefs) and are independently checkable, and the underlying niche-SEO-plus-referral-or-fulfillment model is a real, established local-service business approach. The $700,000/year case study is one specific example the presenter found, not independently verified, and he's explicit that results aren't guaranteed.

name: Compacting recyclable materials with a hydraulic baler, both for better recycling-center payouts and as a paid compaction service for other businesses
cost: Moderate ($690-1,500 depending on size)
what: Buy a hydraulic baler (10 tons of pressure, compacts plastic, cardboard, or textiles into dense bales) to compress your own recyclable material before selling it to a recycling center, since compacted material pays more per load (it saves the buyer transportation and handling costs); separately, offer the same compaction as a paid service to stores, warehouses, and supermarkets that generate cardboard daily but don't have space or budget for their own baler.
pitch: The presenter frames the baler as a profit multiplier rather than just workshop organization equipment, since recycling centers pay more for compacted material, and highlights the underused second income stream: charging other businesses $690-1,500 to compact their own cardboard on-site.
best: Someone already collecting recyclable material who wants better payouts, or willing to offer compaction as a standalone service to local businesses.
truth: Hydraulic balers and their role in improving recycling-center payouts are real, standard industry equipment and practice. No specific personal revenue figures are given.

name: Airbnb and short-term rental turnover cleaning service for property management portfolios
cost: Low startup cost (roughly $1,000 if you already have a working vehicle, or around $5,000 total including a vehicle and supplies)
what: Offer full turnover cleaning for short-term rental (Airbnb-style) properties — not just sweeping and wiping surfaces, but managing linens, restocking guest toiletries, and flagging maintenance issues — targeting property managers who oversee entire portfolios of listings needing service multiple times a week between every guest checkout, rather than standard residential cleaning clients who need service once every week or two.
pitch: The illustrative account describes starting the service part-time on weekends alongside a full-time job before it outgrew that income within three months, then scaling by landing property-manager clients with 20-50 properties at once rather than pursuing homeowners one at a time; a single turnover clean is priced $150-400, and that rate multiplied across dozens of weekly turnovers compounds quickly with a hired team.
best: Someone willing to build relationships with local property managers (who control access to many properties at once) rather than only marketing to individual homeowners, and comfortable eventually hiring and managing a cleaning team to handle the higher frequency this niche demands.
truth: This reads as an illustrative/composite story rather than a verified individual, so treat the specific dollar figures as representative rather than audited. The underlying structural insight — that turnover frequency (multiple cleanings per property per week) compounds revenue much faster than standard biweekly residential cleaning — is a genuine, checkable feature of the short-term rental market that doesn't depend on any one person's specific story.

name: Custom LED neon sign business selling to local businesses and event rental companies
cost: Low startup cost (about $120-200 in materials for a 10-ft sign)
what: Design and build custom LED neon signs using flexible LED neon strip, acrylic backing, and a heat gun for bending, selling locally to bars, salons, and boutiques opening new locations, and to event and photo-booth rental companies who reorder seasonally, rather than competing on price against overseas factories.
pitch: 12-volt LED neon flex runs about $4.94/foot, a 60-watt power supply is $25, acrylic backing is $12-50/sq ft, and a heat gun is a one-time $22 cost — a 10-ft sign costs $120-200 in materials. Market pricing: small signs (12-18in) sell $80-250, medium $180-500, large $400-1,200, or $50-150/foot for simple designs. The presenter calls this the widest profit spread on his list ($5-15/foot in, $50-300/foot out) but warns overseas factories will undercut you below your own material cost on generic designs.
best: Someone comfortable doing custom design work quickly and competing on speed and local relationships rather than price, since the presenter is explicit that competing on generic designs against overseas manufacturers is a losing strategy.
truth: The pricing spread is genuinely attractive, but the presenter's warning is important and easy to overlook: this only works by specializing in fast, custom, local work — trying to compete on standard designs or price against overseas suppliers will fail before it starts.

name: Epoxy garage flooring installation service
cost: Low to moderate startup cost (epoxy materials and application tools; practice runs recommended before charging clients)
what: Apply epoxy resin coatings to garage concrete floors (and later patios, basements, and small commercial spaces) for homeowners converting garages into functional living spaces like home gyms, workshops, or game rooms, mastering one specific installation technique well and building a portfolio of before-and-after photos, since the business sells primarily through visual references and word of mouth.
pitch: The presenter frames the appeal as strong margins (materials cost relatively little compared to the per-square-foot installed price) combined with fast job completion (one to two days per job), and specifically recommends practicing on your own garage or a family member's before charging real clients, since the application technique has a short learning curve but any mistakes remain visibly permanent on the floor.
best: Someone willing to practice the technique thoroughly before taking paying clients, and comfortable building a portfolio-driven, word-of-mouth marketing approach rather than relying on advertising.
truth: The advice to practice on a low-stakes floor first is genuinely important given the presenter's own warning that mistakes are permanent and immediately visible, which could otherwise damage a new business's local reputation quickly. The margin and speed advantages described are real, but building a reputation strong enough to expand beyond garages into commercial spaces will take time and a demonstrated track record.

name: Junk removal service
cost: Low startup cost (lower if you already own a truck)
what: Show up to a customer's home or property, quote the job on the spot based on volume, load unwanted furniture, appliances, or debris into a truck or trailer, and haul it away, getting paid in cash or card immediately rather than waiting on invoicing.
pitch: Zaback frames the U.S. waste collection services industry (projected to surpass $90 billion by 2030) as large enough that small local operators can carve out real income, citing $500 to $1,500 a day in realistic revenue for a single truck and $250 to $300 as a typical job price. He emphasizes that the real growth lever is relationships, real estate agents, property managers, and estate sale companies, since apartment turnover alone runs 40-50% annually and creates a steady pipeline of clearance jobs.
best: Someone who already owns or can access a truck or trailer and is comfortable building referral relationships with property managers, agents, and contractors rather than relying purely on one-off individual customers.
truth: The per-day and per-job revenue figures are Zaback's own stated ranges rather than a single verified case study, though they're specific and consistent with the kind of pricing publicly discussed across the junk-removal industry. The relationship-based growth strategy (property managers, agents, estate companies) is a concrete, actionable, and independently testable approach regardless of the exact revenue figures.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: The consume, apply, educate roadmap to a $10,000-a-month income
cost: Very low startup cost
what: This is a general three-stage framework rather than one specific business, for building a high-income skill into a public, teachable business. Stage one is consuming targeted knowledge (picking one high-income skill like video editing, sales, or design, then learning it from credible creators and communities, not just random content). Stage two is applying it by taking on real, even low-paying, clients to build a track record. Stage three is educating others in that same skill once you've built real experience, through content, courses, or communities.
pitch: Tilbury argues the real money isn't in the skill itself but in eventually teaching it, since an education product (a course, membership, or community) only has to be built once and can be sold repeatedly for predictable, recurring revenue. He frames relatability, being visibly a few steps ahead of your audience rather than a distant expert, as the actual differentiator that gets people to buy from you over someone more credentialed.
best: Someone starting from genuinely little, no capital, no track record, who's willing to spend real time building a skill and a public presence before expecting income, rather than someone looking for a fast, passive result.
truth: The framework itself (build a skill, prove it on real clients, then teach it) is sound and echoes advice from other creators covered elsewhere in this database. Worth knowing: partway through, the video recommends a paid book-summary app and a course-hosting platform (Kajabi) as sponsored plugs, so those specific tool recommendations carry a financial incentive, separate from the underlying framework, which doesn't depend on either product.

name: Running a UV printing service for personalized products across many different businesses, not just phone cases
cost: Moderate to high ($2,199 for the machine)
what: Buy a desktop UV printer (prints on glass, wood, metal, plastic, packaging, and more, with UV-cured ink that resists fading) and offer personalization/printing runs to a wide range of small businesses: personalized bottle openers for a brewery, wooden award plaques for a company, printed cosmetics boxes, engraved puzzles — each production run can be a different client's order.
pitch: The presenter frames the value as: a basic wholesale phone case is cheap, but the same case personalized with a name or photo sells for several times more because it's now unique and incomparable to a generic product — and the same machine and logic applies across many other hard-surface products.
best: Someone comfortable marketing a personalization/printing service to multiple different small business types rather than specializing in one product.
truth: UV printing on hard surfaces is a real, established small-manufacturing capability, and the personalization value-premium described is standard, sound pricing logic. No specific revenue figures given.

name: Short-term rental arbitrage (Airbnb without owning property)
cost: $5,000 to $15,000 to furnish a unit
what: Rent a property from a landlord with their written permission to sublet it, furnish it, and list it on short-term rental platforms; your profit is the gap between what you pay in rent and what you collect in nightly bookings, without ever needing a mortgage or down payment.
pitch: The video estimates $1,000 to $3,000 in profit per unit per month, with some operators managing 5 to 20 units this way, and stresses that systems (automated booking, guest messaging, a rotating cleaning crew, and dynamic pricing software) are what make multiple units manageable.
best: Someone comfortable with the logistics of furnishing and managing a short-term rental, and who can find a landlord willing to permit subletting for this purpose in writing.
truth: This model is real and practiced (often called "rental arbitrage"), but it depends entirely on finding a landlord willing to allow it in writing, many won't, and on local short-term rental regulations, which vary widely by city and can restrict or ban this model outright. The video doesn't mention either of those real constraints, worth researching thoroughly before committing to a lease based on this plan.

name: Amazon Associates affiliate income via YouTube review videos
cost: Free to join, no ongoing fees
what: Join the Amazon Associates program to get a unique tracked link for any Amazon product, then create YouTube videos (talking about or demonstrating products, without necessarily appearing on camera) with those affiliate links in the description, earning a commission on anything a viewer buys on Amazon within 24 hours of clicking through, not just the specific product featured.
pitch: Gottfried's single best piece of advice is to make videos about topics people are actively Googling or searching for on YouTube, since that content earns organic views without needing an existing subscriber base or following, and he notes that a large share of commissions actually come from "secondary sales," other items a visitor adds to their cart beyond the one they originally clicked through for.
best: Someone comfortable creating video content (camera-on or camera-off, talking about products they already know or own) but who doesn't want to build a large following first, since Gottfried's approach relies on search-driven discovery rather than an audience.
truth: Gottfried discloses that videos have worked "head and shoulders above everything else" for him personally compared to photos or social posts, a stated preference based on his own experience rather than a universal claim. The 24-hour attribution window and secondary-sales mechanic are concrete, verifiable facts about how the Amazon Associates program actually works, not marketing claims specific to his own results.

name: Paid online focus groups and user testing
cost: Free to start (just sign-up time; no equipment needed)
what: Sign up on platforms that pay everyday people for their opinions on products and services (the presenter names User Interviews, Respondent, and dscout), applying to daily interview opportunities, most conducted over video calls from home.
pitch: The presenter made $9,000 through this method, applying to about 5-10 opportunities daily even without expecting to be selected for most of them. Sessions pay $40-120/hour, selected slots fill within minutes so speed matters, and payment (via gift card or PayPal) typically arrives within 1-5 days.
best: Someone with reliable internet and video-call comfort who's willing to apply to many opportunities regularly, since selection isn't guaranteed and slots fill fast.
truth: This is a genuine, low-effort way to earn supplemental income with no upfront cost, and the pay rates cited are real for this type of work. Income is inherently inconsistent since it depends on being selected for a limited number of daily opportunities, so it works better as a side income stream than a reliable primary one.

name: Gourmet mushroom growing for restaurant and farmers market sales
cost: Low startup cost (about $260 for an all-in-one starter kit, or $200-800 for a DIY build)
what: Grow gourmet mushrooms (lion's mane and oyster varieties) in a small home setup (tent, humidifier, inline fan), selling on standing weekly orders to restaurants and at farmers markets, taking advantage of the fact that fresh cultivated mushrooms are classified as unprocessed produce in most U.S. states, requiring no permit, cottage food license, or commercial kitchen.
pitch: An all-in-one starter kit with two fruiting kits runs about $260; ready-to-fruit bags cost $5-8/lb, dropping to $2-5/lb if mixing your own substrate. Restaurants pay $8-16/lb (oyster at the lower end, lion's mane at $12-16), while farmers market retail runs $15-24/lb — skip distributors, who only pay $3-6/lb. The presenter frames standing weekly delivery orders of 5-70 lbs as the actual business, warning that a single missed delivery is what loses an account, and that pricing off your own supply cost (one grower's mistake: selling at $5/lb in a market paying $10) leaves money on the table.
best: Someone with space for a small grow tent setup and the discipline to hit consistent weekly delivery schedules, since missed deliveries are described as the fastest way to lose restaurant accounts.
truth: The regulatory finding (no permit needed for fresh mushrooms as unprocessed produce in most states) is a genuinely useful, often-overlooked detail that lowers the real barrier to entry significantly. The business is fundamentally a reliability business — restaurants care more about consistent weekly delivery than about anything else — which is a different skill than growing itself.

name: Custom foam insert fabrication for equipment and product cases
cost: Low startup cost (about $250-550 for foam stock and cutting tools)
what: Cut custom foam inserts that hold tools, electronics, camera equipment, samples, or collectibles securely in place inside cases and shipping boxes, selling mainly to businesses (repair companies, photographers, tool sellers, sales teams) rather than casual individual buyers.
pitch: A beginner setup (foam stock, cutting equipment, adhesives, measuring tools, sample cases) costs roughly $250-550, using sharp knives, cutting guides, templates, or hot wire tools, with more advanced shapes outsourceable while a beginner handles measuring, prototyping, and assembly. The core challenge is precision: an opening too loose lets the product move, too tight and the customer struggles to remove it or the foam tears.
best: Someone with patience for precise measurement and prototyping work, comfortable pursuing recurring B2B clients (a single repeat business client can outweigh dozens of individual customers) rather than one-off consumer sales.
truth: The precision challenge described is real and not to be underestimated — foam insert work has a genuine skill floor around accurate measuring and prototyping, and the presenter's advice to start with simple rectangular/layered designs before attempting complex shapes is sound risk management for a beginner.

name: Snail mail subscription club
cost: Very low startup cost
what: A paid physical-letter subscription, around $10 a month, where a creator writes and mails personal letters, recipes, or art to subscribers each month, no email newsletter, actual physical mail.
pitch: One cited example grew to $60,000 in monthly recurring revenue within 7 months, built entirely through organic short-form video, with no pre-existing following required.
best: Someone with a genuine creative hook or personality who enjoys the tactile, personal-touch side of a subscription business.
truth: The numbers given are specific and credible, 2% churn, the first 1,500 customers coming from a single viral video, which is a good sign. Reliably mailing physical letters at scale, especially internationally, adds real cost and delivery-time considerations most digital subscriptions don't have.

name: AI ghostwriting
cost: Low startup cost
found: Mark Tilbury and Iman Gadzhi (covered independently by both)
what: You use AI tools like Claude, paired with a research tool, to write LinkedIn posts, email newsletters, and ad copy on behalf of founders and creators who know they should be publishing content but don't have time to write it themselves.
pitch: The AI does the heavy lifting, drafting research and a first pass at the writing, while you focus on making it sound like the actual client, not a generic AI voice. Tilbury recommends picking one niche so clients see you as a specialist worth paying more for. Gadzhi covers the same idea independently and rates it a solid, if competitive, option.
best: Someone who already writes reasonably well and is comfortable using AI to speed up research and a first draft, without expecting the AI to replace their own judgment and editing.
truth: Tilbury is fairly upfront that AI only gets you about 75% of the way there, the research and a rough draft. The remaining 25%, taste, editing, knowing what the client would actually say, is a real editorial skill this doesn't remove. Gadzhi's independent take echoes the same caution: results can go well or badly depending on that missing piece.

name: Buy aged/expired domains with existing traffic, then choose the monetization method
cost: Domain purchases from under $50 to several thousand dollars each, plus an optional paid tool subscription
what: Instead of picking a business model first (dropshipping, print-on-demand, AI agency, SaaS, faceless YouTube, Amazon FBA, affiliate marketing), buy an aged or expired domain via marketplaces like Spamzilla that already has organic search traffic, rankings, and backlinks in a real niche, then decide afterward what to sell to that ready-made audience.
pitch: Argues every popular online 'business model' is really just a monetization method, and every one dies at the same point: lack of buyer traffic. Owning a domain that already has traffic and backlinks makes the eventual offer swappable and independent of any single platform or affiliate program change.
best: Someone with some capital to invest in domain purchases and the research skill to vet a domain's real traffic and backlink quality before buying, who wants a ready-made audience rather than building one from zero.
truth: The core insight — audience/traffic is the scarce asset, not the offer — is widely-held, credible online-marketing wisdom. Specific domain-valuation figures cited are third-party tool estimates the presenter himself caveats as not a guaranteed resale price. Buying an expired domain for its rankings/backlinks is an established but real-risk tactic: Google can devalue an old backlink profile after an ownership change, and some niches carry trademark risk, as the source itself flags for one example. The presenter's own paid tool and lead-gen notes page are promoted throughout.

name: Etsy "PNG shop" selling AI-generated clip art and wall art as PDF downloads
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Running an Etsy shop selling cheap AI-generated clip art and printable wall art delivered as a PDF containing a Google Drive download link, built by pulling already-trending design ideas from a trend-research tool and using Claude for the listing copy.
pitch: The presenter shows a real large Etsy shop selling exactly this model as proof of concept, then walks through his own workflow: using a paid trend-research tool to find already-trending design niches, cross-checked against Google Trends for legitimacy, generating matching AI art in an image tool, exporting multiple variations, uploading files to a shared Google Drive folder, building a simple PDF delivery card containing that Drive link, and using Claude only to write SEO-optimized Etsy titles, descriptions, and tags. States this is a volume-and-consistency business, not a one-hit-listing business, and that he is not selling a course.
best: Someone comfortable posting a high volume of low-priced listings consistently rather than expecting one or two designs to carry the business.
truth: The presenter explicitly discloses AI use in his own Etsy listings, as required by Etsy's policy, and states buyers don't seem to mind, a genuinely transparent practice worth noting positively. He states he isn't selling anything in this video, a mild credibility signal, though the specific weekly revenue figures shown are self-reported screenshots, not independently verified. Two paid tools are referenced with affiliate-style links in the description.

name: High-ticket recurring AI agency bundle for one local-service niche, instead of one-off AI websites
cost: Low startup cost (fulfillment outsourced to a developer team for a revenue share)
what: Running a specialized AI agency that sells a bundle of five recurring AI systems to a small number of high-ticket local service businesses in one committed industry niche, rather than selling cheap one-off AI websites to many small clients.
pitch: The presenter argues the AI-website business model breaks down because it's low-ticket, non-recurring, and rapidly commoditized by free tools, and instead recommends committing to a single high-value local-service niche such as roofing, HVAC, solar, or med spas for a minimum of 3-6 months. He sells a bundle of five recurring AI systems addressing specific revenue leaks, including a missed-call voice receptionist, a speed-to-lead follow-up agent, dead-lead reactivation, an internal knowledge assistant, and an AI quoting agent, quantifying each business's dollar losses during the sales call using a framework he calls identify, quantify, prioritize, selling one system at a time starting with the costliest leak, then expanding into the rest with the same client over time.
best: Someone more interested in sales and client relationship management than hands-on technical building, since the presenter explicitly delegates all development work, and comfortable running a structured, numbers-driven sales conversation.
truth: The presenter's own numbers, including per-system pricing of $8,000 to $15,000 upfront plus $2,000 to $5,000 a month, and having helped clients scale to $10,000 to $30,000 a month, are self-reported without account or client verification shown on screen. The core critique of the low-ticket AI-website model, crowded, one-time payment, no recurring relationship, is a reasonable, internally consistent business argument independent of whether his specific numbers are exact. The video ends promoting the presenter's own paid one-on-one mentorship program.

name: Pay-per-lead agency (broker or self-run)
cost: Needs ongoing ad budget (or none, if brokering)
what: Instead of selling marketing services on a retainer, generate qualified leads through Meta ads and a qualifying quiz funnel in a single niche, like life insurance, business loans, or debt settlement, and sell each lead exclusively to a buyer who wants that kind of prospect, or broker leads between existing suppliers and buyers without touching ad spend yourself.
pitch: Robinson argues this beats a traditional retainer agency on two fronts: leads are an easier sell than ongoing "marketing services" because virtually every business owner says yes to more leads, and there are two direct levers to grow profit, raising the price per lead or lowering the cost to generate it. He walks through ten specific verticals with rough sale prices and costs to generate (life insurance around $50 to $60 a lead, mortgage leads $100 to $120, legal leads up to $200 to $250), and recommends beginners start with the lower-risk broker model, sourcing leads from existing suppliers and reselling at a fixed markup, before eventually running their own ad campaigns.
best: Someone with real comfort running or learning to run Meta ad campaigns, or, for the broker path, someone comfortable with B2B cold outreach and negotiating supplier relationships, since neither path is a passive income stream.
truth: Robinson discloses upfront that he's teaching this as a free lead-in to his paid community, and the free version leaves out the detailed funnel templates, scripts, and full campaign structure that are gated behind the paid offer. The specific revenue figures (a $250K+/month agency, 30% average margins) come from his own screenshotted tracking sheet, a more concrete transparency signal than most claims in this space, but still self-reported and not independently audited.

name: Google Search Ads for narrow, problem-specific PDF products
cost: Low to moderate startup cost (ad spend)
what: Selling narrow, problem-specific PDF products, such as a guide for parents dealing with a specific sleep issue, by targeting people already typing that exact problem into Google, using Google Search Ads rather than social media ads.
pitch: The presenter, with 17 years selling digital products, argues Google Search Ads target the most purchase-ready traffic possible, since someone typing a specific, painful search query at any hour is actively looking for a solution right now, unlike social media traffic which has to be interrupted mid-scroll. Recommends picking a highly specific long-tail keyword problem, using the Google Keyword Tool to confirm real search volume, and using AI to draft and self-rate multiple ad headline and description options before choosing the highest-rated ones.
best: Someone comfortable identifying a narrow, specific, painful problem within a broad niche rather than a generic topic, and willing to actively manage a paid ad account rather than relying purely on organic traffic.
truth: The specific example math given, 100 clicks a day, 5 sales at $30 each, is presented as an illustrative scenario rather than the presenter's own verified campaign data. The core strategic argument, that search-intent traffic converts differently than social interruption-based traffic, is a well-established digital marketing principle independent of the specific numbers used to illustrate it.

name: Faceless social media growth funneled into a digital product store
cost: Low startup cost (AI store-builder and content-coaching tool subscriptions; no upfront inventory)
what: Grow faceless social media accounts (Instagram, TikTok, Facebook) around a specific niche using a repeatable content system, then monetize the resulting audience primarily through a low-ticket digital product ($9-29 range) sold from a store built with an AI tool (Instastore.ai), alongside affiliate links and other offers.
pitch: The presenter (Isabella, "Baddie In Business") says she built multiple faceless accounts across different niches to a combined 15 million followers and became a millionaire within two years, reportedly funneling over $10 million through a mix of external monetization (products, affiliate links) and internal platform monetization. She outlines five content rules (raw over polished, keyword-heavy captions, series-based content, combining short- and long-form, and a clear one-line "hero statement" of who you help), and demonstrates AI tools (Instastore.ai for the store, an AI coaching tool called Stanley IG) to speed up content planning and analysis.
best: Someone comfortable being consistently active on social media without showing their face, who's willing to research and repurpose content in a specific niche and treat content creation as a repeatable system rather than a one-off creative project.
truth: The core mechanic (build an audience faceless, sell a low-ticket digital product) is a real and increasingly common pattern, and the specific content-strategy advice is more concrete than most creator-growth content. That said, the "$10 million" and "15 million followers" figures are self-reported and describe results from operating multiple accounts across niches over time, not a single quick win, and the video promotes several of the presenter's own paid tools and a paid coaching community (Viral Wealth) alongside the free advice, which is worth knowing going in.

name: SEO-driven affiliate content site built on topical authority
cost: Low to medium: hosting ~$2-$25/mo, AI-theme builder ~$149 one-time, optional paid SEO tools $100-$200/mo (video argues these can be skipped)
what: Build a personal-brand WordPress site around one narrow subniche (e.g. 'ATV equipment,' 'indoor herb gardening kits') and publish an initial ~20 articles (mostly how-to posts plus a handful of 'best of' product roundups) using AI for subniche selection, keyword lists, and first drafts that the creator edits with personal experience. Add affiliate links once articles get real traffic, join affiliate networks, then negotiate higher commissions or flat sponsorships once you have ranking leverage.
pitch: Presented as the creator's own proven, most successful model — a single site claimed to earn over $1M/year for three years running. The pitch is that going deeper into one narrow subniche than large media sites bother to ('topical authority') is now the dominant Google ranking factor, letting a solo AI-assisted creator outrank major outlets in lower-competition pockets.
best: People willing to commit to 6-24 months of mostly unpaid, consistent publishing before real income appears, who either write in their own authentic voice or heavily edit AI drafts, and who pick a niche with genuine purchase intent and real affiliate programs.
truth: The overall playbook (evidence-based reviews, topical clustering, negotiating commissions with traffic leverage) reflects real, well-documented affiliate-SEO practice. The specific dashboard figures shown are the presenter's own unaudited claims. The video itself admits results are unpredictable post-by-post, that it took roughly five years of continuous publishing to reach these numbers, and that a Google algorithm update once hurt the presenter's own rankings — this is not the fast/passive shortcut implied by 'free 10 hour course' framing.

name: Custom tufted rug business
cost: $250-300 for a complete kit
what: Use a tufting gun, a handheld tool that shoots yarn at high speed onto fabric stretched on a frame, to create custom rugs with a logo, character, or design, a process that would take weeks to weave by hand but takes hours with the tool.
pitch: A small rug costs around $20 in materials and sells for $60-250 depending on size and design, with a customer base spanning barbershops and streaming studios wanting branded entryway rugs to individuals wanting a rug with their pet's face or kid's name. The process itself is described as inherently viral content: posting a video of a rug being made tends to generate orders on its own without needing to actively find clients.
best: Someone who enjoys hands-on, visually satisfying craft work and is willing to post the process on video, since the content itself is described as doing much of the marketing.
truth: The cost and price figures are consistent with what's publicly listed for tufting kits and finished custom rugs elsewhere, a reasonable range. No specific named operator or verified sales figures are given, so the income potential is illustrative rather than demonstrated by a real case study.

name: Selling AI-generated Meta ad creative to brands that are running too few ads compared to their competitors
cost: Low (Claude subscription, an AI image/video tool like Higgsfield)
what: Use the free Facebook Ad Library to find brands running noticeably fewer ads than their direct competitors (a signal they can't produce creative at scale); use Claude for ad copy, hooks, and angles, and an AI image/video tool (Higgsfield) for the visuals, feeding Claude a competitor's proven, long-running ad as creative inspiration to build sample ads for the underspending brand before ever contacting them; approach the founder or ad manager with several free finished samples already made, rather than pitching the idea cold.
pitch: The presenter demonstrates this live on a real brand (a keyboard company running only 20 ads worldwide versus a competitor's 700), generating finished sample ads in minutes and framing unsolicited, already-built samples as the strongest way to get a response; he scores this 14/25 on his own scorecard (ease 3, speed 3, validated 5, competition 3, long-term 5) and cites charging $1,000-5,000+ per brand depending on scale.
best: Someone willing to learn ad strategy and AI image/video tools, comfortable doing unsolicited prospecting work (building free samples) before landing a client.
truth: The Facebook Ad Library is a real, free, public research tool, and AI-generated ad creative is a real, current capability demonstrated live. The presenter's own pricing and scorecard reflect his stated experience but aren't independently audited, and the video promotes a specific AI tool's affiliate signup and his own paid training/coaching.

name: Local courier and delivery service for small businesses with recurring contracts
cost: Very low startup cost (your own vehicle; practically no inventory required)
what: Offer same-day local courier and delivery service for small businesses that need documents or small packages moved quickly within a city — the presenter highlights pharmacies, law firms, and dental clinics as target customers — pursuing monthly recurring contracts with a handful of businesses rather than competing for individual one-off delivery requests, and organizing routes by grouping deliveries by area and time window.
pitch: The presenter frames the medical and legal sectors as the biggest opportunity, since confidentiality and punctuality matter more to those clients than price, allowing higher rates than a generic courier service, and notes that just three or four well-organized monthly contracts can cover vehicle and fuel costs before any additional delivery counts as extra profit.
best: Someone with a reliable vehicle who wants recurring B2B delivery contracts rather than one-off gig-app-style deliveries, and who's comfortable pitching directly to medical, legal, and other small business offices.
truth: Targeting recurring monthly contracts with a small number of businesses (rather than competing for scattered one-off deliveries against big shipping companies) is a sound way to build predictable income in a normally low-margin category, and the specific niche framing (confidentiality/punctuality-sensitive sectors) is a genuinely useful positioning angle. Landing those first few contracts still requires direct outreach and building trust with each business individually.

name: Solar panel cleaning service
cost: Very low startup cost ($500-$800 for equipment, no license required in most states)
what: Clean the dirt, dust, pollen, and bird droppings that build up on residential and commercial solar panels, restoring lost power output, using a soft-wash or low-pressure hose system, a squeegee, and a water-fed pole, typically sold as a one-to-two-times-a-year recurring package.
pitch: Zaback frames the sales pitch around reframing the service: it's not just panel cleaning, it's recovering lost energy output on an investment that may have cost the homeowner $20,000-$30,000, since regular cleaning can boost power production by 10-20% in dirty conditions. He cites the solar panel cleaning industry being valued at $1.22 billion in 2025 and projected to reach $2.57 billion by 2035, with especially strong opportunity in high-solar-adoption states like Arizona, Texas, California, and Florida.
best: Someone in a solar-dense region looking for one of the lowest equipment costs and least regulatory friction on this whole list, ideal for someone wanting a simple, low-overhead recurring-revenue service.
truth: The industry valuation and growth figures are cited as third-party market research rather than Zaback's own data, and no specific individual operator's income is given for this particular idea, unlike several others in the video, so there's no personal case study to weigh here. The core value proposition (dirty panels underperform, cleaning restores output) is a straightforward, physically verifiable claim independent of any specific revenue projection.

name: Microgreens growing for restaurant wholesale accounts
cost: Low startup cost (about $500-700 for a garage-scale rack with grow lights and shelving)
what: Grow microgreens (sunflower, pea shoot, amaranth) in trays under grow lights in a garage or spare room, selling on standing weekly wholesale orders to two or three restaurant accounts rather than trying to build a broad consumer customer base.
pitch: Heavy-duty 10x20 trays start around $15, and a full garage-scale rack with shelving and grow lights runs $500-700. Real cost per tray (seed, medium, power, water, packaging, and labor at $20/hour) comes to $5-7. Sunflower trays retail $18-22, pea shoots $16-20, amaranth $25-35, with margins running 66-79%. Growers target $25-40/tray wholesale — 10 trays/week nets roughly $108, 50 trays/week around $490. The presenter warns that overwatering or dense sowing causes mold that can wipe out an entire tray (and miss a delivery) in a single afternoon.
best: Someone with reliable indoor growing space who's willing to build 2-3 solid restaurant relationships and treat consistent delivery as the core of the business rather than trying to sell broadly to consumers.
truth: The margins are genuinely attractive and the space/equipment requirements are modest, but the presenter is honest that the failure mode is both fast and total — a single contaminated tray from overwatering can take out an entire week's crop and cost you the account, so this rewards careful, consistent process more than volume.

name: Epoxy garage floor coating funded by selling jobs before buying equipment
cost: Moderate startup cost to learn (roughly $2,000 for manufacturer training) with equipment financed via client deposits rather than upfront purchase
what: Apply high-performance epoxy/polyaspartic coatings to garage concrete floors (grinding down the old surface, repairing cracks, then applying a decorative, chip-resistant finish that lasts 20-30 years), but bootstrap the expensive commercial equipment (a concrete grinder can cost over $20,000) by first landing paying clients through targeted local ad campaigns showing dramatic before/after transformations, collecting a 50% deposit upfront, and using those deposits to rent the grinding equipment day-by-day from a local supply shop rather than buying it outright — only purchasing owned equipment once enough client-funded profit has accumulated.
pitch: A garage floor job typically takes a two-person team one day and homeowners pay $4,000-7,000 per garage given the finish's longevity, with the illustrative account citing about $1,800/month in ongoing truck-and-gear overhead against up to $60,000 in monthly revenue at scale. The presenter is candid that early mistakes are costly and specific: underestimating how long a job will take when old sealant resists the rented equipment can turn a projected two-day job into two weeks, so testing the concrete's hardness and moisture before quoting became a hard-learned, now-standard step.
best: Someone willing to invest in proper technique training before taking paying jobs (this trade has a real, visible failure mode if botched) and comfortable using a sell-first, equipment-later financing sequence rather than buying expensive gear speculatively.
truth: This reads as an illustrative/composite story rather than a verified individual, so treat the specific dollar figures as representative rather than audited. A similar epoxy garage flooring entry already exists in this database from a different producer emphasizing portfolio-building and practicing on a low-stakes floor first; this version's distinct, checkable contribution is the deposit-funded equipment rental strategy for bootstrapping expensive gear, and the specific concrete-testing lesson learned from a near-failure.

name: AI-leveraged bookkeeping and payroll services
cost: Low startup cost, software subscriptions only
what: Document-heavy, recurring back-office services, bookkeeping, medical billing, or payroll, where AI now handles much of the document processing, letting one person serve more clients than before. No accounting license is required, just tool fluency and a chosen niche.
pitch: This work is recurring by nature, businesses need it every month, not once, and AI tools have lowered the manual workload significantly compared to a few years ago.
best: Someone comfortable learning bookkeeping or payroll software and who wants steady, recurring client relationships over flashier project work.
truth: This is a solid, learnable option, though it's more operational than strategic compared to something like fractional executive work. It requires real comfort with financial recordkeeping, not just general business sense.

name: Leasing and servicing commercial ice machines for bars, restaurants, and hotels
cost: Moderate to high (cost of ice machine units to lease out)
what: Lease commercial ice machines to bars, restaurants, and hotels on an all-inclusive monthly contract covering service calls, repairs, and bi-annual maintenance, so the business never has to deal with an ice machine failure themselves (which tends to happen during a busy Friday night rush, not a quiet afternoon).
pitch: Leasing companies charge $75-500/month per unit; the presenter frames what's really being sold as the guarantee that a breakdown becomes someone else's emergency, which is why customers rarely negotiate on price.
best: Someone comfortable managing a fleet of leased equipment and coordinating repair/maintenance service (whether performed personally or subcontracted).
truth: Commercial ice machine leasing with bundled maintenance is a real, established equipment-service model in the food service industry. Pricing figures are general industry ranges, not a specific verified case study.

name: Residential pressure washing service
cost: $75 (rental) to $3,200 (own equipment)
what: Pressure wash driveways, siding, and other exterior home surfaces for homeowners, starting with a rented machine and scaling up to owned commercial-grade equipment as the work becomes steady.
pitch: The video walks through starting with a $75 weekend rental from a home improvement store, landing two of six neighborhood doors knocked on, and making $210 in a single afternoon, then scaling to three jobs a Saturday at $300 to $500 per job with 20-50% profit margins after buying a $3,200 commercial setup.
best: Someone who wants a genuinely low-cost way to test a service business on weekends, comfortable with physical outdoor work and basic neighborhood marketing.
truth: This is one of the more checkable, concrete ideas in the video; the starting cost (a rental) is real and low enough that most people really could test this in a single weekend, a good sign for a beginner-friendly idea. The claimed monthly totals depend on booking a consistent volume of jobs every single weekend, which takes real ongoing marketing effort the video doesn't detail.

name: AI-written done-for-you content service for busy professionals
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Use ChatGPT or Claude to write newsletters, blog posts, LinkedIn posts, and social captions on behalf of busy professionals, like doctors, plumbers, or founders, who know they should be publishing content but don't have the time, then hand them the finished, ready-to-post material.
pitch: Hamilton frames the pitch around convenience rather than the writing itself: professionals will pay for speed and ease, having someone hand them scripts and posts ready to use rather than having to write anything themselves. The pitch to a client is built around not making them do any of the work, not requesting information they'd need time to gather.
best: Someone comfortable picking a specific professional niche (rather than writing generically for anyone) and willing to do the outreach to land a first few clients.
truth: This is a fairly general pitch without a specific pricing example, client acquisition story, or verified case study in the video, more of a suggested direction than a tested playbook. The underlying mechanic, using AI to draft content a professional would otherwise pay a ghostwriter for, is straightforward enough to test cheaply before committing to it as a primary offer.

name: Private AI assistant built for a solo expert (consultant, solicitor, advisor)
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Build a private AI assistant for a solo professional, a consultant, solicitor, or financial advisor, by loading their past proposals, FAQs, and other documents into a Claude Project, then instructing it to answer questions and draft new proposals only in that person's own voice and only from their own material.
pitch: Hawksworth demonstrates the entire build in a couple of minutes: start a Claude project, drag in roughly 20 past proposals and FAQs, and give it a single instruction to answer only from the documents provided and ask a clarifying question if the answer isn't there. He suggests charging around £1,500 to build it and £300 a month to maintain it as their workflow grows, framing the value as multiplying the expert's own existing knowledge rather than replacing them.
best: Someone comfortable working with solo professionals who already have a body of past work, proposals, FAQs, case files, to draw from, since the tool is only as good as the material it's trained on.
truth: The pricing (£1,500 build, £300/month) is the presenter's own suggested figure, not a documented sale. The underlying build process itself, a Claude Project scoped to a specific person's documents with a narrow instruction, is simple enough to verify and replicate directly.

name: AI automation agency
cost: Low to moderate startup cost
what: Build backend automation systems, beyond just phone calls, things like workflow automation, data syncing, or repetitive task elimination, that replace manual work for businesses.
pitch: This is pitched as the higher-ticket version of AI services: rather than one tool doing one job, you're diagnosing a business's operational pain points and building a broader system, which supports charging more per client.
best: Someone comfortable with more technical, hands-on implementation work than a simple one-tool service, and who enjoys diagnosing a business's specific bottlenecks.
truth: Gadzhi is candid that the real need is genuine and the upside is there, but execution and managing multiple moving systems for a client can get tricky in ways a simpler single-tool service doesn't.

name: Buying and reselling Costco liquidation returns
cost: A few hundred to a few thousand dollars per pallet or lot
found: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
what: Buy pallets or individual units of Costco customer returns and liquidated merchandise through the B-Stock auction platform, researching resale value on Facebook Marketplace or comparable retail listings before bidding, then resell the items individually online, through Facebook Marketplace for larger items or Whatnot live auctions for smaller consumable goods.
pitch: Chris Koerner challenges an experienced reseller, Shannon, to help him turn a starting bankroll into $10,000 profit in 10 days flat, buying returned and liquidated Costco merchandise through the B-Stock auction platform at pennies on the dollar (a $3,400 gazebo for $200, an $1,800 furniture set for $200) and reselling it on Facebook Marketplace and, for smaller items like food and drinks, through live-auction platforms like Whatnot.
best: Someone with storage space (a garage or a small storage unit) and access to a bit of starting capital, who's comfortable researching resale prices before bidding and willing to learn category-specific quirks like appliance grading and model research.
truth: This same buy-liquidation-and-resell pattern shows up repeatedly across WAH creator content, sourcing returned or excess inventory well below retail and reselling it piece by piece, which is itself a signal that the underlying model genuinely works, not just a one-off story. What makes this version distinct: a Costco-specific sourcing angle through the B-Stock auction platform, a named experienced mentor walking through live bid research in real time, and the Whatnot live-auction resale channel for smaller consumable goods, a genuinely different selling mechanic than one-off Marketplace listings. Koerner is candid that categories like appliances and electronics require real category-specific knowledge to avoid getting burned, and that not every item resells quickly, sometimes you cut the price and take a loss just to free up storage space.

name: Monetizing a curated Spotify playlist
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Build a Spotify playlist in a specific genre or mood, grow its followers, and monetize it by giving independent artists a way to get their songs placed on it in exchange for payment.
pitch: There are two ways to charge for this: directly billing artists a flat fee per song placement, or running it as a Patreon-style membership where artists pay a small monthly fee for the chance to submit music for consideration. Tilbury prefers the second, since it's more passive (income arrives monthly without per-song negotiation) and feels more honest, since you're only picking songs you'd genuinely include rather than accepting anyone who pays. At $5 a month, 1,000 subscribed artists would be $5,000 a month.
best: Someone with a genuine ear for a specific music genre or mood who's willing to put in the upfront time to build a playlist's following before it has real placement value to artists.
truth: Tilbury is upfront that the direct pay-per-placement version violates Spotify's terms of service, and flags it as a real downside of that approach, not just a minor caveat, which is a good transparency signal. The Patreon-membership version he prefers doesn't have that problem. No specific real-world case study or dollar figures are given for either approach, so the $5,000-a-month math is illustrative math, not a demonstrated result.

name: Manufacturing woven clothing labels for small clothing brands that can't meet big suppliers' minimum order requirements
cost: Moderate to high ($3,600 for the machine)
what: Buy a narrow fabric loom (weaves logos, not just text, using 16 frames; also makes ribbons and trim) and produce woven clothing labels for small/emerging clothing brands, who typically hit a wall trying to source labels: big suppliers require minimum orders of 10,000+ units, imported, with 6-week lead times, which doesn't work for a small brand's first run.
pitch: The presenter argues labels are legally required on garments (size, fabric, washing instructions) so no clothing brand can sell without them, and frames the real business as recurring: a brand releases a new collection every few months and needs new labels every single time, making you 'part of how that brand exists' rather than a one-time vendor.
best: Someone willing to serve small/emerging clothing brands specifically, since large brands already have established label suppliers.
truth: Woven label requirements and the minimum-order gap for small clothing brands are real, well-documented pain points in the apparel supply chain. No specific revenue figures given; pricing and margin framing are the presenter's general claims.

name: Custom work apron and tool roll sewing business
cost: Low startup cost (about $500-800 for a heavy-duty sewing machine and materials)
what: Sew canvas or denim work aprons, knife rolls, brush rolls, and tool organizers designed around the specific equipment carried by a particular trade (barbers, baristas, florists, bakers, tattoo artists, mechanics, woodworkers), selling both personalized individual pieces and small matching batches to businesses.
pitch: A realistic setup (a strong sewing machine, cutting tools, canvas or denim, webbing, hardware, thread, labels, packaging) runs $500-800. The presenter recommends choosing one profession and talking to people who actually do that work to learn what they carry every day, rather than designing 10 generic styles upfront, since heavy fabric and multiple pockets require accurate cutting and consistent stitching that a badly-placed pocket can ruin.
best: Someone with real sewing skill (or willing to develop it for heavy fabric work) who's willing to research one specific trade's actual daily-carry needs before designing a product.
truth: The advice to build around a real workflow for one profession, rather than a generic multi-purpose apron, is a genuinely sound way to create a product people actually value over a novelty item — but it requires real sewing competency with heavy materials, which isn't a trivial skill to pick up quickly.

name: Buying, renting, and flipping mobile homes
cost: Moderate startup cost (buying a used mobile home, typically needing minor repairs)
what: Buy used mobile homes at a discount (often needing minor cosmetic repairs), fix them up with simple upgrades like paint, flooring, and kitchen updates, then either rent them out for steady monthly income or resell them at a markup — starting within an already-established mobile home park (where land is rented separately, lowering the initial investment) rather than buying land outright.
pitch: The presenter frames this as combining two income streams in one business — ongoing rental income if you keep the property, or a lump-sum resale profit if you flip it — and recommends starting with one or two units in an established park before considering land ownership, once more experience and capital are available.
best: Someone comfortable with basic home repair and renovation work (or managing contractors who do it), willing to start small within an established mobile home park before taking on land ownership.
truth: Starting within an established park to avoid the added cost and complexity of land ownership is sound, practical advice for lowering the initial investment in this business. Rising demand for mobile homes as a more affordable housing option is a real market tailwind, but this still requires real capital for the initial purchase and repairs, and success depends on realistic repair-cost estimation and local rental or resale demand, which the video doesn't detail specifically.

name: Field inspection contract work
cost: Very low startup cost (a smartphone and a car)
what: Work as a contract field inspector for companies that need someone local to visit a property or business, take photographs (of a vehicle, building exterior, or specific condition), and submit them, typically for insurance, compliance, or verification purposes.
pitch: One presenter describes earning $75 for a roughly 20-minute inspection (a short drive plus photographing two company vehicles), working with a company called Metro Inspections. That specific company is no longer accepting new inspectors, but the presenter notes other similar inspection companies are actively hiring.
best: Someone with a reliable car and smartphone who wants flexible, quick-turnaround local gig work that doesn't require any specialized skill or equipment beyond basic photography and following instructions precisely.
truth: This is a genuinely low-barrier gig with fast per-job payouts, though per-job pay ($75 for 20 minutes in the example given) means meaningful income requires taking on a steady volume of jobs, and availability of inspection companies actively recruiting will vary by location and over time.

name: Resin and wood serving board business selling wedding and corporate gifting bulk orders
cost: Low startup cost (about $500-700 for a full setup including hardwood, torch, sander, and respirator)
what: Make resin-and-hardwood serving boards and wall art pieces (skipping lower-value resin jewelry and coasters, which the presenter says are impulse buys with no reorder pattern), selling primarily through wedding and corporate gifting bulk orders and boutique home goods retailers buying wholesale.
pitch: Clear casting resin runs about $19/quart ($51/gallon); a 12x8in serving tray costs about $37 in materials and sells for $150-200, while large wall art pieces cost about $147 in materials and sell for $450-600 — both using the same $51 gallon of resin, meaning the price gap is almost entirely labor and perceived value, not materials. The presenter's key warning: cheap resin or a sloppy mix ratio causes yellowing under UV months after the sale, which comes back as a refund request and a bad review long after the money was spent.
best: Someone with patience for a precise, technical craft process who's willing to pursue bulk gifting orders (weddings, corporate) and wholesale retail relationships rather than one-off retail sales.
truth: The materials-vs-labor cost breakdown is a genuinely useful pricing insight, and the specific warning about resin quality and yellowing is the kind of hard-won detail that prevents an expensive mistake — a board that fails months after sale costs both the refund and the reputation damage.

name: Fire extinguisher testing and inspection route
cost: Low to moderate startup cost
what: Inspect and tag fire extinguishers for offices, restaurants, warehouses, and apartment buildings on the legally required annual inspection schedule, building up a recurring route of accounts over time.
pitch: Every commercial building is legally required to get its extinguishers inspected on a set schedule, and fire marshals actually check for the tag, which means the law itself does the sales pitch for you. Once you're inspecting a building's extinguishers, switching to a new inspector means a customer has to re-explain their whole building to someone new, which the presenters say makes accounts unusually sticky once you land them.
best: Someone comfortable with slower, longer commercial sales cycles who's willing to build up a large route of low-ticket accounts over time rather than looking for one big score.
truth: The presenters are honest that this sits mid-list specifically because it isn't high-ticket per visit, so building meaningful income requires a genuinely large route and patience with commercial sales cycles. They note it's a fragmented market with no dominant national brand, a real and checkable structural fact about the industry.

name: Running a nationwide basketball hoop installation booking service using local subcontractors in each city
cost: Low (a simple booking website; no equipment needed since subcontractors provide their own)
what: Build a website and brand focused solely on basketball hoop installation, operating across many states/cities by dispatching each job to a local handyman/contractor subcontractor rather than doing installations personally; grow the client base partly through B2B outreach to companies that sell basketball hoops online, offering to handle installation referrals for their customers.
pitch: The presenter found a real company (basketballhoopinstall.com) operating this exact model across Arizona, Colorado, Georgia, Indiana, Kansas, and more, using local subcontractors in each market rather than a single local crew.
best: Someone comfortable managing a network of subcontractors across multiple markets and doing direct B2B outreach to hoop retailers rather than performing installations themselves.
truth: This is a real, verifiable company operating exactly as described, and the subcontractor-dispatch-plus-B2B-referral model is a sound, replicable structure for a narrow installation niche. No specific revenue figures are given for this particular business.

name: Purifying free used cooking or motor oil into biodiesel feedstock with a mobile filtration machine
cost: Low ($865 for the machine)
what: Buy a portable oil purification machine (100-micron filter, 75kg, fits in a pickup truck) and collect used cooking oil from restaurants (who are eager to have it hauled away rather than clogging drains or paying disposal fees) or used motor oil from repair shops, filter it clean, and sell the purified oil as biodiesel feedstock to farmers, transportation companies, and local fleets, or as filtered motor oil to repair shops.
pitch: The presenter frames this as a business where the raw material comes to you for free and the supplier is grateful, highlighting that the same machine serves two separate markets (cooking oil for biodiesel, motor oil for repair shops) depending on which filter setting you use.
best: Someone comfortable with a mobile, route-based collection model, willing to build relationships with restaurants and repair shops as ongoing suppliers.
truth: Used cooking oil and motor oil purification for biodiesel/resale is a real, established waste-arbitrage niche. No specific personal revenue figures are given.

name: Amazon Influencer Program: short product review videos on Amazon listings
cost: Free to join (requires an active social media account to apply)
what: Record short review or demo videos for products you've already purchased from Amazon, upload them to your Amazon Influencer account, and earn a commission whenever a shopper watches your video directly on that product's Amazon listing page and then buys, without ever needing to post the videos to your own social media.
pitch: Gottfried, three months into this specific program at the time of filming, made about $70 in profit his first month simply reviewing products he already owned, then jumped to roughly $1,400 in his second month after switching strategy: using a data tool to check how many other influencer videos already exist for a given product (since Amazon only displays about five per listing) and prioritizing products with little existing video competition over ones already saturated with 100-plus competing videos.
best: Someone who already owns a range of Amazon-purchased products and is comfortable recording brief, simple review or demo videos, understanding that visibility (getting into the limited top-five video slots) matters more than production quality.
truth: Gottfried is specific that his own $70-to-$1,400 jump came from a single tactical shift (competition-checking before choosing which products to review), a concrete and replicable insight rather than a vague growth claim. The application does require proving an existing active social media account, even though the ongoing work happens entirely on Amazon's platform, a real and sometimes confusing requirement worth knowing upfront.

name: Window cleaning service for homes and businesses
cost: Very low startup cost (~$500 for basic equipment)
what: Clean windows for homes, storefronts, and office buildings, starting with a basic kit (squeegee, mop, bucket, ladder, cleaning solution) and quoting jobs by square footage and number of stories, with the option to sell recurring quarterly packages to homeowners and monthly contracts to commercial clients.
pitch: Zaback cites an average residential job of around $550, meaning six jobs in a day already crosses $3,000 in gross revenue, and profiles an Arizona operator who did $392,000 in a year with a small subcontractor team, starting with just $500 in equipment. He specifically highlights commercial accounts (restaurants, retail, offices) as more valuable than residential ones because they prioritize reliability over price shopping and will commit to standing monthly contracts.
best: Someone comfortable quoting jobs quickly over the phone once they know their pricing formula, and willing to pursue commercial accounts specifically for the more stable, less price-sensitive recurring revenue they offer over one-off residential jobs.
truth: The $392,000/year figure is a specific, named example (an Arizona operator using a subcontractor team) rather than an anonymous claim, though it represents one successful operator, not a typical or guaranteed outcome. The distinction Zaback draws between residential (price-sensitive, one-time) and commercial (reliability-focused, recurring) customers is a genuinely useful and independently testable segmentation for anyone starting this business.

name: Mobile car detailing service
cost: About $2,700 for starting equipment
what: Travel to customers' homes or workplaces to clean and detail their vehicles, interior and exterior, using portable equipment rather than operating from a fixed shop location.
pitch: The video cites a Reddit thread (with posted Square payment receipts as evidence) from an operator claiming $3,700 to $4,200 in monthly revenue detailing cars out of a home garage, at $150 to $300 per job with a 60-80% profit margin.
best: Someone comfortable with physical, hands-on outdoor work and willing to build a weekend booking schedule, without needing a storefront or employees.
truth: The Square receipt screenshots mentioned in the source material are a genuinely better transparency signal than most claims in this video, real payment platform data, not just a stated number. That said, this is still a secondhand Reddit account relayed by the video, not something independently verified here. The margins and price points described are broadly consistent with what real mobile detailers charge.

name: Guitar setup and repair service for gigging musicians and teachers
cost: Low startup cost ($133 for a basic setup kit, or $250-400 for a complete kit)
what: Perform guitar setups and repairs (action adjustment, fret leveling, nut work, full refrets) for gigging musicians and music teachers, who need this service 2-4 times a year as instruments respond to seasonal temperature and humidity changes and typically stick with one trusted repairperson once they find one.
pitch: A basic setup kit (action gauge, straight edge, radius gauges) runs about $133, though the presenter notes it's usually missing truss rod wrenches; a genuinely complete kit with nut files, fret rocker, feeler gauges, and wrenches runs $250-400. Local shop rates: basic electric setup $60-120, acoustic $70-140, fret level and dress $150-300, nut work $60-120, full refret $300-600. Per-job material cost is typically just a set of strings and a small part.
best: Someone with (or willing to develop) genuine guitar-tech skill, who understands that trust and repeat business come from doing quality work on a musician's primary instrument, not from marketing.
truth: The recurring-need mechanic (2-4 times per year, driven by seasonal humidity changes) and the low per-job cost make this a genuinely attractive margin business, but it requires real technical skill that takes time to develop — this isn't a business you can start competently with just the tool list alone.

name: High-ticket digital product affiliate marketing via webinar, book-a-call, or nurture funnels
cost: Very low startup cost (mainly time; an optional ad budget for paid traffic)
what: Become an affiliate for other people's high-priced digital products ($1,000-$5,000+ courses, coaching, and software) rather than cheap physical goods, earning 50-70% commissions through networks like Digistore24, ClickBank, JVZoo, and WarriorPlus. Rather than sending a cold affiliate link straight to a sales page, route prospects through one of three 'selling mechanisms': a live webinar, a 'book-a-call' funnel where a hired closer works the prospect on a Zoom call, or a multi-day 'nurture sequence' of value-packed videos that builds trust before the pitch.
pitch: The argument is that commissions on cheap physical products (a $20 t-shirt, a $50 gadget) are too small to matter, while digital products carry near-limitless perceived value and high commission rates, so a handful of $1,000+ sales a month beats thousands of tiny ones. The 'selling mechanism' is framed as the real skill: no matter how good the product or the traffic, sending someone straight to a $2,000-$5,000 sales page without first building trust through a webinar, a live call, or a nurture sequence simply won't convert.
best: Someone comfortable creating consistent content or running ads, and willing to either host webinars, hire/become a phone closer, or build out a multi-video email/DM sequence, rather than just dropping a bare affiliate link.
truth: The presenter's claimed ~$3 million in lifetime affiliate sales is self-reported with no independent verification, and the video funnels toward his own free masterclass. The webinar and book-a-call mechanisms in particular require either real public-speaking/sales comfort or budget to hire a closer, which raises the actual effort and cost well above the 'just sell someone else's stuff' pitch.

name: Domain investing and instant lead-gen microsites for underserved local searches
cost: Very low startup cost (roughly $10 per domain)
found: Chris Koerner (guest on Marketing Against the Grain)
what: Speculatively buying inexpensive, often-overlooked domain names, either to build instant, AI-generated lead-generation microsites for underserved local-service search terms, or to hold and resell premium address-based domains to developers and businesses.
pitch: The guest argues .com domains are still wildly underpriced relative to their potential value. He demonstrates the method with a pressure-washing example: search a service-plus-city combination, and if there's real search volume but only one or two competitors rather than a crowded market with paid ads and a map pack, buy a cheap exact-match domain, use AI tools to quickly build a generic lead-gen site, then wait. Once inbound leads start arriving, give the first few away free to a real local business to build trust, then start charging per lead once traffic proves out. A parallel version: use AI to generate lists of the most common street names and building-address numbers in a market, buy the matching domains in bulk for a few dollars each, and hold them to resell later to real estate developers or property buyers who want that exact address online.
best: Someone comfortable with a low-cost, patience-based numbers game, many cheap domains, most going nowhere, a few paying off, rather than someone wanting a single fast-moving business.
truth: This is a live, off-the-cuff brainstorm between two marketing hosts and a serial entrepreneur guest, not a personally tested case study with real revenue numbers from either idea, so treat the specific dollar figures as illustrative reasoning rather than demonstrated results. The core logic, buying long-established, still-undervalued domain inventory, is presented as a real and repeatable opportunity independent of the specific example given.

name: Native mobile app built end-to-end with a no-code AI app builder, published to the App Store
cost: Low to moderate startup cost (AI app-builder subscription plus a $99/year Apple developer account)
what: Building a native iOS mobile app from scratch using a no-code AI app-building tool, describing the desired app in plain language and iterating through each build phase, then publishing it through Apple's App Store submission and TestFlight beta process.
pitch: The presenter walks through cloning the core concept of a well-known app as a demonstration case, feeding a chain of specific prompts one at a time into a no-code AI app-building tool: design and navigation first, then a key feature, then a backend database for data persistence. He also covers deploying a companion legal and landing page and the real mechanics of Apple's App Store submission process, including the developer fee, TestFlight beta testing, and the review wait time.
best: Someone comfortable directing an AI tool through an iterative build process and willing to navigate Apple's actual app-submission requirements, not just build a prototype and stop there.
truth: This video's tool recommendation is a paid sponsorship, which the presenter discloses directly, so the specific platform choice should be weighed with that in mind, though he does explain his reasoning, native hardware access like the camera, for picking it over alternatives. The example app is a demo and practice clone, not the presenter's own live revenue-generating business, so no income figures are given or implied for this specific build.

name: Niche life-event Etsy templates (funeral and baby-announcement digital downloads)
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Creating Canva-designed, customer-customized digital templates for specific life events, such as funeral announcements and pregnancy or baby announcements, sold as instant digital downloads on Etsy.
pitch: The presenter argues under-covered, less-glamorous niches like funeral products see steady, year-round demand with less seller competition than more popular decorative niches. A shop can build a full catalog around one product type by producing color and theme variations of the same template rather than constantly designing new products.
best: Someone comfortable with Canva and willing to research a specific, less-obvious life-event niche rather than competing in the most crowded general categories.
truth: The specific dollar figures shown, including a roughly $332-a-month funeral template and a shop scaling to about $3,000 a month largely on themed variations, come from a third-party Etsy research tool that estimates sales from visible signals, not confirmed transaction data, so these are directional rather than exact.

name: A validation trick for any Amazon KDP book idea
cost: Near-zero cost
what: Before writing any book, check the Amazon Best Sellers Rank (BSR) of similar, already-published books in that topic. A BSR under roughly 80,000 signals there's real, ongoing demand for that kind of book, worth knowing before you invest the time to write one.
pitch: This isn't a business on its own, it's a simple, free way to de-risk any print-on-demand book idea, coloring books included, before spending time on it.
best: Anyone considering the Amazon KDP coloring book idea, or any similar print-on-demand book concept, who wants a cheap gut-check before committing time.
truth: The presenter also promotes a paid AI writing tool alongside this technique, but the validation method itself works fine using just a free Chrome extension and Amazon's own listings.

name: Coaching existing YouTubers on monetization and growth
cost: Low startup cost, needs your own credibility
what: Coach existing YouTubers who already have an audience and expertise, in this case a creator teaching the Amazon KDP publishing model, on monetization, operations, and hiring, packaged as a paid course plus coaching program.
