pitch: In a named, on-camera case study, Hummus describes taking his client Sean's channel from around 100,000 subscribers to over 300,000, more than tripling AdSense income to $22,000 a month, growing course revenue to over $500,000 a month, and landing a single affiliate commission of $73,000 along the way.
best: Someone who already has real, demonstrable expertise in a specific area of business or content growth to coach others in, since this model depends entirely on already having that credibility.
truth: This is Hummus's own paying client, interviewed together on camera, which is a stronger transparency signal than a third-party retelling, but it's still a single promotional case study from the coach's own business, not an independently audited result. Building a coaching business requires you to already have real expertise in a specific niche, which isn't something this idea creates for you.

name: AI receptionist reseller for local businesses
cost: ~$297/mo for a HighLevel software plan (covers unlimited clients)
what: Install a white-label AI phone receptionist (built on the HighLevel platform) for local businesses that miss calls — plumbers, dentists, landscapers. The AI answers every call 24/7, holds a natural conversation, books appointments, and takes caller info. Charge the business a flat $397/month.
pitch: Cites a 411 Locals study claiming only ~40% of small-business calls get answered by a real person and that 85% of people who hit voicemail never call back, so a missed call is a plausible lost job. A US Census Bureau survey is cited finding only 18% of businesses use AI at all, mostly large ones, framing small local businesses as an underserved, easy market. The seller installs and operates existing tools rather than building anything new.
best: Someone comfortable pitching and onboarding local business owners who wants to resell an existing white-label tool rather than build their own AI product from scratch.
truth: The cited statistics are attributed to real sources but not independently verified here. The underlying mechanic — reselling white-label AI voice automation to local businesses monthly — is a real and growing service model. The recommended software platform is the presenter's own affiliate link (with a bundled template pack unlocked through it specifically), though the business model itself doesn't require using that particular link.

name: Print-on-demand apparel shop using AI "node-based" design workflows
cost: Low startup cost
what: Running a print-on-demand apparel shop (e.g. on Etsy) built around AI "node-based" design pipelines: you connect a reference design, an AI text-generator node, and an AI image-generator node so that changing one global theme prompt automatically remixes dozens of unique, on-trend design variations, which are then prepped (upscaled, background removed, sized to a product) and listed using reusable presets with AI-generated SEO titles, descriptions, and tags.
pitch: The presenter argues that researching what's already proven to sell, then using an AI node-based pipeline to remix those proven concepts into original variations, lets him go from a niche idea to finished, ready-to-sell product listings in 10 to 20 minutes, a dramatic speed-up from years of manually designing print-on-demand products by hand.
best: Someone who already has some print-on-demand or design background, or is willing to learn a real design-canvas/node-based tool rather than a single AI chat prompt, and who is comfortable focusing on one product type and iterating designs at real volume rather than a handful of one-off listings.
truth: The presenter has sold, by his own account, a few million dollars of print-on-demand products over six years, and he's promoting his own software (Listing View) and paid community (Merch Makers) throughout, so there's a clear commercial incentive behind the specific tools named. That said, the underlying process, researching proven designs, using AI to remix them into original variations, prepping files properly, and batch-listing with presets, is a real and teachable workflow independent of which specific tool runs it. He also repeatedly and explicitly warns against copying another seller's design directly, a genuine legal/platform-ban risk worth taking seriously.

name: Free AI-built Shopify dropshipping store using storebuild.ai and Zendrop
cost: Very low startup cost ($1/month Shopify promo, free AI store builder)
what: Use a free AI tool (storebuild.ai) to auto-generate a themed Shopify dropshipping store in about 30 seconds, complete with a pre-selected niche, color scheme, and banner, then connect a Zendrop supplier account so winning products are pre-loaded and automatically fulfilled when a sale comes in.
pitch: Rabin, who says he's run e-commerce stores for over 7 years and generated 250,000+ orders, presents this as the same premium theme his own brand (which he says scaled to $3.9 million) uses, available for free through a discounted Shopify trial ($1/month for 3 months). He walks through picking a niche, generating the store, linking Zendrop as a supplier, and turning on auto-fulfillment, positioning the main remaining work as marketing and product testing rather than building or fulfillment.
best: Someone who wants a dropshipping store live quickly without design or development skills, and who is prepared to invest time and money afterward into marketing and paid ads, since the store itself doesn't sell anything on its own.
truth: The store-building and fulfillment automation genuinely works as described and removes real technical barriers to starting. The $3.9 million figure is Rabin's own reported result and isn't independently verified, and the video doesn't cover the ad spend, testing, and iteration that a result at that scale would actually require — the free store is a starting point, not a shortcut to that level of revenue. It's also a promotional walkthrough for a specific paid tool stack (storebuild.ai, Shopify, Zendrop), not a neutral comparison of options.

name: Faceless AI explainer-video YouTube channel using competitor-modeling and AI production tools
cost: Low startup cost (free tools; paid AI tool optional)
what: Building a faceless YouTube channel using AI tools to post explainer-style videos in a chosen niche, monetized through standard YouTube ad revenue.
pitch: The presenter argues most beginners fail because of weak channel trust signals, so recommends rebranding an old channel or properly optimizing a new one's SEO settings before posting. The core method is finding proven ideas by studying two or more competitor channels' top-performing videos, checking total views and views-per-hour to confirm the topic still has real demand, then using an AI tool to generate a script modeled on competitors' structure and pacing, an AI voiceover, and AI-generated visuals timed to the voiceover's natural pauses.
best: Someone comfortable following a fairly technical, multi-tool AI workflow and willing to research proven-idea patterns from competitor channels rather than inventing original content from scratch.
truth: The presenter shows on-screen analytics claiming over $35,000 in the last 28 days and averaging around $31,000 a month, but these are self-reported dashboard screenshots, not independently verified. The video is careful to frame the method as modeling a competitor's proven structure and pacing rather than copying their actual video, though the line between the two is something a viewer should judge for themselves. The channel-trust and SEO advice covered is standard, legitimate YouTube practice.

name: AI-generated animal coloring book PDFs sold via Payhip
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Creating simple AI-generated animal coloring book PDFs, using Claude for the book plan and prompts, an AI image tool for the illustrations, and Canva for layout, sold as an instant digital download via Payhip.
pitch: The presenter shows a real earnings screenshot and walks through a four-step system: have Claude generate a full book plan, cover concept plus black-and-white and colored prompts for every page, in one prompt, generate matching images in a free AI image tool using a top-selling Etsy listing's cover as visual inspiration rather than a copy, assemble the pages in Canva with white space left for coloring, then publish as a digital product on Payhip, which handles delivery and payment automatically. Also demonstrates making a short slideshow-style preview video alternating black-and-white and colored versions of each page to boost buyer confidence.
best: Someone comfortable treating this as an ongoing catalog business, multiple books, multiple niches, rather than a one-off project, since consistency across many books is what compounds results.
truth: The single-day earnings figure is shown via a self-reported dashboard screenshot, not independently verified, and no broader monthly or annual context is given for how typical that day was. The presenter is candid that AI-generated content draws criticism from some viewers and addresses it directly rather than hiding from it. A paid mentorship is promoted at the end.

name: AI vibe-coded digital products sold through your own branded online shop
cost: Very low startup cost (AI coding tool plus a domain)
what: Research proven-selling digital templates and tools (using public sales-data tools to see exactly how many times a competing product has sold and for how much), "vibe code" a functional version using an AI coding platform like Hostinger Horizons, then sell it through your own branded .shop domain online store rather than a crowded third-party marketplace like Etsy.
pitch: The presenter shows real, specific examples to justify the approach: a finance-niche budget tracker template that's sold over 20,000 times for more than $400,000, and a life planner niched down specifically for neurodivergent people with ADHD that's sold over 22,000 times for more than $350,000, arguing that competitive niches (finance, health, productivity) are actually good signals of real demand as long as you niche the specific problem down far enough. She argues against selling on marketplaces like Etsy specifically because of listing and transaction fees, competition burying your listing, and the risk of account suspension, versus owning your own store with a .shop domain and full customer data control.
best: Someone comfortable using an AI coding tool with detailed, specific prompts (rather than vague requests) to build an actual functional product, not just a static file, and willing to set up their own branded storefront rather than relying on marketplace traffic.
truth: The specific $400K and $350K product examples are shown as public sales data from other sellers, not the presenter's own results, and she doesn't demonstrate her own product's sales figures within the video. She recommends Horizons specifically because it integrates with her own store-building workflow and is, by her account, one of the least expensive AI coding platforms, worth noting as a product preference rather than a neutral recommendation.

name: Low-ticket digital course as a near-passive income stream
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Package your existing knowledge into a low-priced digital course ($27 to $197), sold through an automated sales page and email sequence rather than live sales calls, so that once it's built it keeps generating revenue with essentially no ongoing fulfillment work from you.
pitch: Romero compares seven income models she's personally used, one-to-one coaching, high-ticket done-for-you services, low- and mid-ticket courses, affiliate marketing, brand deals, and joint ventures, and argues the low-ticket course model is the only one that gave her real passive income: she made $30,000 to $40,000 a month during a 90-day maternity leave without touching the business. Her reasoning is structural: no sales calls, no fulfillment, and it scales without needing more of her time, unlike the high-ticket, done-for-you offers that required a large team and heavy sales-call involvement.
best: Someone with real expertise or a track record in something specific who's comfortable creating an automated sales funnel once, rather than someone who prefers ongoing client relationships or high-touch coaching.
truth: Romero is candid about the tradeoffs of every model she covers, including admitting she got tempted into building a high-ticket, done-for-you offer that grew her team but not her margins the way she expected, a genuinely balanced account rather than a highlight reel. She promotes her own paid course (the AI Product to Profit Builder) partway through, worth knowing given how much of the video builds toward that pitch.

name: Building a niche Facebook photo page monetized through Facebook's Content Monetization program
cost: Very low (an AI image generation tool, free Facebook Page creation, optional basic photo editor)
what: Pick one narrow, highly visual niche (cozy cabins, vintage cars, tiny homes), validate demand by checking for existing large Facebook pages in that niche, create a public Facebook Page around it, generate original AI images with a specific, detail-rich prompt (not generic), lightly edit each image to make it feel human-made, post one per day with a short caption ending in a question to drive comments, and apply to Facebook's Content Monetization program once the page hits roughly 5,000-10,000 followers with real engagement.
pitch: The presenter reports over $14,000 in one month from Facebook content monetization (mostly PDF sales plus the photo program) and walks through the mechanic: Facebook now pays for original photos and text posts, not just video, but has cracked down hard on reposted or lightly-edited content since 2025, so the images must be genuinely original. He gives a specific 90-day, one-post-a-day plan with a weekly review step, and is upfront this is a slow-build strategy, not a fast-cash scheme.
best: Someone willing to commit to a consistent 90-day daily-posting habit in one visual niche, comfortable writing detailed AI image prompts and doing basic photo-editing polish, patient with a slow initial ramp.
truth: Facebook's content monetization program and its original-content enforcement rules are real and match public information from Facebook's creator resources, and the described mechanics are consistent with how the platform's recommendation system is known to work. The specific $14,000/month figure is self-reported and unverifiable, payout thresholds and eligibility vary by country and change over time (the video itself warns not to trust fixed numbers), and it ends by funneling viewers to a paid course for the full system.

name: Building websites and lead-capture automations for local businesses that don't have one, with a monthly hosting retainer
cost: Very low startup cost (AI tools for prospecting, plus website/automation tools like Claude, WordPress, or Canva)
what: Use an AI tool to scrape Google Maps or business directories for local businesses (especially trades like plumbers, roofers, landscapers, and salons, where up to 45-56% still lack a website) that have no website or only a broken/basic one, then pitch and build them a simple site with a lead-capture form or AI-driven automation (e.g. a WhatsApp/form-based agent), charging around $500 upfront plus a recurring $50-75/month hosting and maintenance fee since you retain control of their hosting.
pitch: The presenter argues the real opportunity isn't a saturated $80 Fiverr website gig but a mid-market position ($500, above the race-to-the-bottom price but below $5,000 agency rates) sold on the basis of "you never have to think about this again," using AI to build a targeted prospect list (business name, contact info, missing-website status) from a given postal code rather than cold-searching Google Maps by hand, then reaching out with a Loom video demo before ever discussing price, and adding a small monthly hosting fee to turn a one-time job into recurring income.
best: Someone comfortable with direct outreach (email, DM, or cold call) to local business owners, and willing to build a simple sample website or automation on spec to demonstrate value before pitching price.
truth: The core premise — a meaningful share of small local trade businesses genuinely lack a website — is broadly plausible and the recurring-hosting-fee structure is a real, sound way to turn a one-time build into repeat income. The presenter doesn't cite an independent source for the specific 27%/45-56% figures, so treat them as approximate rather than verified statistics, and landing the first few clients still requires real outreach and sales skill that the video doesn't walk through step by step.

name: AI-designed print-on-demand Etsy store
cost: Low startup cost (Etsy's $15 setup fee, plus enough cash or credit to cover printing costs until Etsy pays out)
what: Use free AI chatbots to brainstorm clothing designs and Google's free Flow tool to generate the actual artwork, then list the designs on print-on-demand apparel through Printify, sold via an Etsy storefront. Printify charges the manufacturing cost per sale; Etsy pays out the sale price minus its own fees once the item ships.
pitch: Sarah runs this business herself and is candid that it isn't entirely free to run, despite the AI tools themselves being free: Etsy has a one-time $15 setup fee, and because Etsy doesn't release the sale proceeds until after the item ships, you need to be able to front the manufacturing cost (roughly $9 on a $20 shirt in her example) before you're reimbursed. For anyone without even that small amount of float, she points to Printify's own free pop-up storefront tool as a genuinely $0 alternative to Etsy, which pays out as a royalty after Printify covers its own production cost.
best: Someone comfortable with basic AI image generation and willing to either front a small amount of production cash on Etsy, or accept a smaller, simpler storefront through Printify's free option instead.
truth: Sarah discloses she runs a successful version of this business herself, which is a real credibility signal, but also means she has a direct financial interest in recommending the specific paid tools she promotes alongside this content (a Canva Pro affiliate link and her own paid course). The core mechanics of the business (AI design plus print-on-demand fulfillment) don't require either of those paid products to work.

name: AI instant quote/estimate generator for contractors and other quote-first businesses
cost: Low startup cost (Claude access to build the pricing-rules document and intake form logic)
what: Convert a contractor or quote-based business's real pricing structure (base rates, labor, add-ons, often scattered across the owner's head and a personal spreadsheet) into a document Claude reads as pricing rules, then build a short 5-6 question customer-facing intake form whose answers feed those rules to generate a clean, branded estimate delivered by email same-day, with a booking link embedded directly in the estimate so the customer can convert immediately — sold to contractors, roofers, remodelers, landscapers, movers, and law firms who quote work before doing it.
pitch: The sales math: a contractor sending 12 quotes a month and closing 3 who speeds up quote delivery from days to same-day can realistically close 2 more of those 12 (going from 3 to 5), which at a $2,500 average job is an extra $5,000/month — meaning a $2,000-4,000 build pays for itself within weeks. The underlying insight is that slow quote turnaround (the classic "I'll get back to you" that becomes a kitchen-table typing session at 9pm) loses jobs the contractor mistakenly attributes to being outbid on price.
best: Someone targeting service businesses where quotes are genuinely customized (not fixed-price) and slow turnaround is a believable, provable pain point, comfortable extracting an owner's informal pricing logic into a structured document.
truth: This is customer-facing (the end customer fills out the form and receives the estimate directly), which differs from a similar existing entry in this database built as an internal tool for a business's own employees to use — different mechanic, different buyer experience. The $5,000/month projected gain is the presenter's illustrative math from assumed conversion improvements, not a verified case study with a named client's actual before/after numbers.

name: AI-generated printable wall art on Etsy
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Creating AI-generated printable wall art sold as digital PNG or PDF downloads on Etsy, where the customer prints and frames the artwork themselves, using Claude to analyze a bestselling listing's images and generate prompts for an AI image tool to create an inspired-but-different set of designs.
pitch: The presenter shows real examples earning $145 to over $4,000 a month from printable wall art bundles, one shop having made about $600,000 total. He demonstrates screenshotting a top-selling listing, having Claude analyze it and generate several unique, not copied, image prompts, feeding those into an AI image tool, then using a custom cropping tool Claude builds on request to instantly generate all the different print-size dimensions customers expect, cutting what would normally take weeks of manual resizing down to seconds.
best: Someone comfortable directing AI tools iteratively to get a genuinely distinct result rather than a close copy, and willing to build out a full size range for every listing, since top sellers all offer multiple dimensions.
truth: The presenter is explicit he doesn't want to just copy an existing listing and iterates the AI prompts specifically to make the result look different, worth noting as a good practice signal, though the underlying method, studying a competitor's exact images as the starting reference, sits closer to the line than pure independent design and is worth being thoughtful about. The specific revenue figures shown come from each listing's own public Etsy sales data.

name: Building single-purpose micro-utility websites monetized with display ads, using AI to build and market them end-to-end
cost: Very low (free using Google's Antigravity IDE or a Claude Code subscription; free ad networks to start before qualifying for AdSense)
what: Give an AI a vague prompt about your own job, hobbies, and daily annoyances, and ask it to generate 20 single-purpose micro-utility website ideas ranked by likely traffic, validate real search demand for a handful of favorites in Google Trends, then have Claude Code or Google's free Antigravity IDE build and deploy the site end-to-end (including signing up for an ad network and inserting ad slots) from a single prompt, monetizing through a low-traffic-friendly ad network first before graduating to Google AdSense once traffic grows.
pitch: The presenter cites several real examples of single-purpose utility sites (a temporary-email generator, a 'weird Amazon products' site, a link-outage checker) earning $2,500-$39,000/month purely from display ads on very simple pages, and argues such sites can also be resold later at 25-40x monthly earnings; he demonstrates the entire build live, including his own previously-built metadata-removal tool as a real personal example.
best: Someone comfortable directing an AI coding assistant conversationally rather than writing code themselves, willing to validate an idea's search demand before building rather than guessing.
truth: Simple utility websites monetized by display ads are a real, long-standing internet business model, and the specific named examples are genuine existing sites, though their exact revenue figures are unverified claims relayed from the sites' own founders. The video promotes the presenter's own paid 'Wealth Academy Pro' community for a prompt-injection 'skill' and free-token workaround, and separately teases a paid 'Mythos AI' tool, so those specific add-ons are sales funnels rather than required parts of the core method.

name: Ghostwriting for founders' personal brands by training Claude on their voice using a structured content database
cost: Very low (a Claude subscription, a free Notion account)
what: Build a simple Notion database per client containing their YouTube transcripts or interviews, writing style notes, top-performing content, personal stories, and ideal customer profile, then feed that database to Claude whenever writing so it can draft in the founder's actual voice (getting roughly 60-70% of the way there automatically), adding a human editing pass to finish it; target founders of businesses that already make real money (not solo coaches or agents) who post consistently on LinkedIn or X but get poor engagement.
pitch: The presenter, who writes his own YouTube scripts and other copy using this exact Notion-plus-Claude system, calls this the easiest and cheapest AI side hustle to start, scoring it 22/25 (ease 4, speed 5, validated 5, competition 3, long-term 5), and cites pricing anywhere from $500/month on the low end to $2,000-3,000/month, or a percentage of revenue for top performers.
best: Someone with strong writing/editing instincts willing to study a client's voice and content deeply rather than producing generic AI copy.
truth: AI-assisted ghostwriting using a structured reference database is a real, sound, and increasingly common workflow, and the presenter's own use of it for his own content lends direct personal credibility. Pricing figures are the presenter's own stated ranges from his network, not independently verified, and the video promotes a free companion Claude skill and his own paid training.

name: Fully remote cleaning agency that dispatches jobs to independent subcontractors
cost: Very low startup cost (under $1,000 for a booking website and phone/booking software)
what: Run a home cleaning company entirely remotely by never employing cleaners directly: build a booking website and run local search ads to capture inbound customer calls, quote and book the jobs yourself (or via phone software), then match each job to vetted independent cleaning subcontractors who already own their own equipment and drive to jobs from their own homes — collecting the customer's payment upfront, paying the subcontractor their fixed cut, and keeping the 30-40% margin in between without ever cleaning anything yourself.
pitch: The illustrative account frames the core competitive edge as simply answering the phone: testing ten local competitor cleaning companies on a Saturday morning found seven didn't pick up at all, and immediate answering plus instant booking converted more than half of inbound calls into booked jobs — no cleaning skill or physical presence required from the business owner, since the entire value-add is fast response, reliable dispatch, and vetting subcontractors.
best: Someone who wants a genuinely location-independent business and is comfortable operating as a broker/dispatcher rather than a hands-on service provider, with the discipline to vet and manage a network of subcontractors reliably.
truth: This reads as an illustrative/composite story rather than a verified individual, so treat the specific dollar figures as representative rather than audited. The core insight — that many local service businesses lose bookable customers simply by not answering the phone promptly — is a genuine, well-documented pattern in local-service marketing independent of this particular narrative; building a reliable subcontractor network and maintaining service quality without direct oversight is a real, non-trivial operational challenge the story doesn't dwell on.

name: Custom picture framing and shadow box business
cost: Low startup cost (about $450-750 for a mat cutter, joining tools, and frame stock)
what: Assemble custom picture frames, matted photographs, certificate frames, wedding keepsakes, and shadow boxes for sentimental or unusually-sized items, sourcing pre-cut frame lengths rather than milling raw wood, and selling both to individuals and to businesses (photographers, artists, interior designers) needing multiple pieces in a consistent style.
pitch: A controlled setup (mat cutter, joining tools, saw or miter equipment, clamps, measuring tools, backing materials, starter frame stock) costs $450-750. The presenter emphasizes accuracy at every stage since a slightly out-of-square frame creates visible gaps, and recommends starting with smaller standard formats before attempting large, fragile, expensive-to-ship pieces.
best: Someone with a careful, detail-oriented approach who wants to build a business around trust — the presenter notes this works best when customers trust you with items they wouldn't hand to a discount framing shop.
truth: The trust-based framing (pun intended) of this business is accurate: custom framing customers are often handling sentimental, irreplaceable items, so quality and care matter more here than in most craft businesses on this list, and that's a real differentiator from big-box framing shops.

name: Running a commercial window-cleaning business by hiring crews rather than doing the height work yourself
cost: Moderate (equipment for crews plus insurance/bonding for height work; you don't need to do the work personally)
what: Sign annual commercial window-cleaning contracts for office buildings and hospitals, hiring and paying two-person crews to do the actual height work while you handle sales and contract renewals; the business avoids competition because most people are deterred by the physical fear-of-heights factor of the work itself, not by cost or complexity.
pitch: The presenter cites an operator running three two-person crews specializing only in hospitals and office buildings who bills $300,000/year without doing any height work himself, paying $400-1,000 per work day per contract that renews automatically every January.
best: Someone comfortable managing and paying crews for physically demanding work, willing to sell annual contracts to commercial property managers.
truth: Commercial window cleaning is a real, established trade with genuine annual-contract recurring revenue, and delegating the physical work to hired crews while owning client relationships is a standard small-business-scaling structure. The $300,000/year figure is one presenter-cited example, not a guaranteed outcome, and insurance/liability requirements for height work are a real operational cost not detailed here.

name: Medical courier service using your own vehicle
cost: Very low startup cost (your own car; no special equipment)
what: Deliver medical supplies, specimens, and blood drive collections between facilities using your own vehicle, contracting with medical courier companies rather than general delivery apps like DoorDash or Uber.
pitch: Presenters in the video report earning $1,200-2,500 per week doing pickups and deliveries (blood drive collections, medical supply loads) using their own car, describing the pay as noticeably better than a regular job or standard gig-delivery apps.
best: Someone with a reliable vehicle who wants delivery-style gig work with better pay than standard rideshare/delivery apps, and who's comfortable handling sensitive medical materials responsibly.
truth: The pay rates described are genuinely higher than typical gig-delivery apps, which makes sense given the specialized, time-sensitive nature of medical deliveries. This kind of courier work typically requires passing a background check and sometimes specific certifications (e.g., handling biohazard materials) that aren't detailed in the video, so expect some onboarding requirements beyond just signing up.

name: Rug tufting business selling custom commissions to interior designers
cost: Low startup cost (about $300-450 for a complete tufting kit)
what: Make custom tufted rugs using a cut-pile tufting gun, monk's cloth, and backing materials, selling primarily to interior designers commissioning custom pieces for clients rather than direct-to-consumer buyers, who the presenter says won't sustain the business at a viable price point.
pitch: A tufting gun runs about $225, with a complete kit (gun, frame, monk's cloth, glue, tools) at $300-450. Materials per rug run about $65 (yarn $27, cloth $13, latex glue $11, backing $8, packaging $6). A 2x2ft rug sells for around $220 at $55/sq ft, suggesting a $155 margin — but the presenter is explicit that a beginner's first several rugs are practice, not sellable inventory, often costing 3-4x more to make than buying a finished rug, meaning real break-even starts around the fourth through eighth rug against a $420 setup cost.
best: Someone willing to treat the first several rugs as paid tuition rather than income, and to pursue interior designer relationships for custom commissions rather than relying on individual consumer sales.
truth: The presenter's honesty about the practice-rug cost curve is valuable and often missing from craft-business hype — budgeting for several unsellable early attempts before turning a profit is a more realistic starting expectation than most tufting content gives.

name: Merch by Amazon print-on-demand t-shirts
cost: No upfront cost
what: List t-shirt (and other apparel) designs for sale directly on Amazon through its Merch by Amazon program. There's no inventory to buy upfront: you upload a design, pick colors and a price, and Amazon prints, ships, and handles customer service, paying you a royalty per sale.
pitch: Tilbury frames this against the traditional route of pre-printing shirts in bulk (multiple colors and sizes) and hoping they sell, which risks money on stock that doesn't move. Merch by Amazon removes that risk entirely since nothing is printed until it's actually purchased, and it also gives you access to Amazon's existing customer base instead of needing to build your own audience or attend events to sell in person.
best: Someone with design skills (or comfortable directing AI tools to generate designs) who wants to test apparel ideas without tying up money in inventory that might not sell.
truth: The illustration used, a friend who pre-printed thousands of shirts and could only capitalize on one design that took off, is a real anecdote but a single example, not a data set. Worth knowing separately: Amazon requires all designs to be either fully original or properly licensed, so using copyrighted characters or logos without permission isn't just against Merch by Amazon's rules, it's a real legal risk.

name: Running a recurring monthly shoe-cleaning pickup-and-delivery service using an industrial washing machine
cost: Low ($680 for the machine, one of the cheapest on the list)
what: Buy an industrial shoe washing machine (six brushes, hot air drying, UV/ozone sterilization, 8 pairs/hour) and instead of opening a walk-in shop, offer a monthly subscription pickup service: once a month, collect a family's shoes from their home, clean and disinfect them, and return them within a few days, removing the hassle of the customer having to remember, carry, and drop off shoes themselves.
pitch: The presenter argues the obvious walk-in-shop model misses the real opportunity: people don't mind paying, they hate the hassle, so a recurring pickup subscription converts a one-time sale into a recurring payment that doesn't require re-convincing the customer every time.
best: Someone comfortable running a local pickup/delivery logistics operation rather than a storefront.
truth: Industrial shoe cleaning machines and pickup-subscription service models are real, and the hassle-vs-cost distinction is sound consumer-service reasoning. No specific revenue figures given.

name: ATM placement business
cost: About $2,000 or more per machine
what: Buy and place ATM machines in local businesses like nail salons or convenience stores, earning a fee on every transaction, and scale by adding more machines over time.
pitch: A real example is cited of someone turning a $2,100 first machine into an $8 million a year company over time.
best: Someone based in the U.S. who's comfortable with local relationship-building and doesn't mind managing physical equipment across multiple sites.
truth: This relies on a single case study, which may not be typical, and it requires physically placing and maintaining machines in person, so it isn't a remote or location-independent business.

name: Running a licensed commercial elevator maintenance contract business
cost: High (requires real licensing and training, typically working under a certified program first)
what: Get licensed and trained in elevator maintenance (typically working under an existing certified program before signing your own contracts), then hold annual maintenance contracts required by law in every state; a small building's contract runs $3,500-5,000/year while a commercial high-rise can run $12,000-20,000/month.
pitch: The presenter is explicit this isn't a weekend side hustle given the real licensing barrier, but frames that barrier as exactly why existing operators have waiting lists instead of marketing budgets, citing Massachusetts fining $100/day for an elevator operating without its required inspection.
best: Someone willing to invest real time in licensing/certification for a genuine skilled trade with a high barrier to entry but correspondingly high contract values.
truth: Mandatory elevator inspection/maintenance laws are real and codified, and the cited Massachusetts penalty reflects genuine regulatory enforcement. This is one of the higher-barrier items on the list, which the presenter states upfront rather than glossing over.

name: Notary loan signing agent
cost: Under $400 (state notary commission plus signing agent certification)
what: Become a certified notary and loan signing agent, then get hired by title companies, escrow companies, or signing services to meet home buyers or refinancing homeowners in person to witness and notarize the paperwork involved in a real estate closing.
pitch: The video cites a CNBC report calling this one of the highest-paying side hustles in America, up to $200 an hour, for appointments that typically take about an hour and pay $75 to $200 each, requiring only a state notary commission ($50-$100) and a signing agent certification course (about $200).
best: Someone who wants a genuinely low-cost, credential-based entry point with a clear certification path, comfortable scheduling and traveling to in-person appointments, often evenings and weekends around closing schedules.
truth: This is a real, well-documented gig economy role (signing services and title companies do hire independent notary signing agents), and the certification path and cost described are accurate to how someone would actually get started. Building a steady stream of signing appointments generally requires getting listed with signing services and building a reputation, which takes time the video doesn't address; the per-appointment pay is real, but consistent volume isn't guaranteed from day one.

name: Pool cleaning and maintenance service
cost: Very low startup cost (a few hundred dollars for equipment)
what: Provide weekly pool maintenance, skimming the surface, brushing walls, occasionally vacuuming the floor, and adding chemicals as needed, for residential customers who don't want to maintain their own pool or risk it turning green and unusable.
pitch: Zaback cites the U.S. pool cleaning and maintenance market at $26.77 billion in 2025, projected to reach nearly $40 billion by 2030, and notes that most residential customers pay $100 to $150 a month for weekly service, a naturally recurring relationship since a neglected pool creates an urgent, visible problem the homeowner wants solved.
best: Someone in a warm-climate state (Florida, Texas, California, Arizona, and similar) willing to build a weekly route, since retention in this business is described as strong once a homeowner trusts a reliable cleaner.
truth: No specific individual case study or income example is given for this particular idea in the video, unlike several of the others, so the pricing and market-size figures are the only data points to evaluate rather than a personal account. The core mechanic (weekly visits, chemical costs scale with actual accounts rather than being paid upfront) is specific enough to verify independently before committing capital.

name: Pinterest-to-Amazon affiliate pin marketing
cost: Free to low ($0 for Pinterest business and Amazon Associates accounts; time cost for pin design)
what: Create a Pinterest business account linked to an Amazon Associates storefront (Pinterest auto-applies affiliate tags and disclosures), then post pins organized around product clusters (e.g. 'Amazon office chair must-haves') linking to Amazon, a blog article, or a YouTube video, with multiple visual angles per cluster.
pitch: Pinterest is framed as an underused 'visual search engine' rather than a social network, where individual pins can reach large view counts with barely any followers because the algorithm surfaces pins to searchers directly, needing no on-camera presence or long-form writing.
best: People who enjoy or are willing to learn basic visual/graphic design and want a low-friction, faceless way to drive Amazon affiliate clicks without first building a blog or YouTube audience.
truth: The Pinterest-Amazon integration is accurate as described. The cited example (one board with 238,000 monthly views) is an anecdotal screenshot, not a representative average. Amazon's own commission rates are low (roughly 1-10%) with a short cookie window, so this works best as one layer of a broader strategy rather than a standalone plan.

name: Desktop laser engraving business for personalized gifts
cost: $200-300 for the machine
what: A desktop laser engraver that etches a name, phrase, or design onto everyday objects (tumblers, cutting boards, keychains, plaques) across more than 150 materials including wood, leather, acrylic, and painted metal, controlled from a phone and requiring no artistic skill.
pitch: A $5 tumbler engraved with a name can sell for $20, and an $8 cutting board with a phrase can sell as a gift for $35, since personalized items are described as rarely getting price-bargained by buyers. The customer base spans anniversary and corporate gifts to cafes and barbershops wanting branded signage, with predictable seasonal demand spikes around Christmas, Valentine's Day, and graduations.
best: Someone looking for a low-skill personalization business with wide material versatility and genuine gift-giving-season demand spikes.
truth: The cost and price figures are consistent with what's publicly available for this kind of engraver and its typical products, a reasonable range. No named operator or verified sales record is given, so the specific income math should be treated as illustrative rather than a demonstrated case study.

name: Building a pressure-washing business around recurring annual contracts instead of one-off jobs
cost: Low ($1,500-4,000 for a pressure washer)
what: Buy a pressure washer and offer sidewalk, facade, and parking-lot cleaning, but structure the business around annual maintenance contracts with corporate buildings and condominiums rather than chasing one-off residential jobs each week, turning it into predictable recurring income.
pitch: The presenter frames the annual-contract model as the key difference between an unpredictable side hustle and a real business, noting demand holds up regardless of the economy since commercial properties are contractually obligated to keep storefronts clean.
best: Someone comfortable with sales calls to property managers and building owners to win annual maintenance contracts, not just one-time homeowner jobs.
truth: Pressure washing is a well-established, low-barrier service business, and shifting from one-off jobs to annual contracts is sound, widely-used advice for reducing income unpredictability in any local service business. No specific revenue figures are given for this particular business type in the video.

name: Custom mug sublimation business for corporate and event gifting
cost: Low startup cost (about $550-750 for a mug press and sublimation printer setup)
what: Produce personalized sublimated mugs for individual gifts and, more importantly, for repeat business customers like real estate agents (closing gifts), companies (employee welcome products), and schools or clubs needing several matching pieces delivered by a fixed date.
pitch: A complete sublimation setup (mug press, compatible printer, ink, paper, thermal tape, blank mugs, test materials, protective boxes) runs $550-750. The presenter stresses that production only begins after order approval, keeping finished inventory low, and that consistency (matching height and color across a bulk order) matters more to repeat business clients than having hundreds of different designs.
best: Someone who can commit to consistent, professional execution on bulk business orders (matching every logo's size and color exactly) rather than treating this as a one-off novelty gift shop.
truth: The presenter's framing around consistency and dependable delivery for repeat business clients (versus just having a wide design catalog) points to what actually differentiates a sustainable small operator from a random online seller in a genuinely crowded product category.

name: Dog treat baking business selling to pet boutiques and farmers markets
cost: Very low startup cost (packaging and labels run 30-80 cents/unit; uses equipment most kitchens already have)
what: Bake dog treats (the presenter's example: peanut butter biscuits) using standard home baking equipment, and sell them to pet boutiques and at weekly farmers markets, while navigating that dog treats are regulated as pet food in many states rather than falling under simpler cottage food laws.
pitch: A dozen peanut butter biscuits cost $1.15-2.05 all-in and sell for $8-12/dozen standard, $10-16 decorated, with gift boxes going $18-35 — about $8.40 profit per dozen at a $10 price point. Six dozen at a market nets around $50; 10-15 dozen nets $85-125. The presenter flags a regulatory detail almost nobody checks: dog treats are classified as pet food, not covered by cottage food law in many states, and some require a commercial feed license with AAFCO nutrient testing even for home-kitchen production.
best: Someone with basic baking equipment already at home who's willing to research their specific state's pet food regulations before their first sale, and who wants pet boutiques and market regulars as repeat customers.
truth: The regulatory warning is the single most important piece of information here — treating this like a standard cottage food business without checking state pet-food rules first is a real, easy-to-miss legal risk, not just a formality.

name: Selling print-on-demand T-shirts through Amazon Merch on Demand, focusing on specific sub-niches instead of broad topics
cost: Very low (free to join Amazon Merch on Demand; a copyright-free commercial-use T-shirt design tool)
what: Join Amazon Merch on Demand and upload T-shirt designs (phrase-based joke/niche shirts); Amazon creates the product listing, handles printing, shipping, and customer service as orders come in, paying the designer a split of the profit per sale. Use a copyright-free, commercially-licensed design tool to quickly create designs without needing Photoshop skills, and focus on narrow sub-niches within a broader topic (not just 'fishing shirts' but 'fly fishing,' 'deep-sea fishing,' 'ice fishing' separately) rather than one generic category, to reduce competition per design.
pitch: The presenter describes this as the first income stream that ever worked for him after being laid off at 18, discovering it passively earned money in the background of his part-time job with no ads or active marketing required, and says it built the foundation that all nine of his other income streams grew out of.
best: Someone willing to create many design variations across specific sub-niches rather than a few broad designs, comfortable with a slow passive-income buildup rather than instant results.
truth: Amazon Merch on Demand is a real, established print-on-demand marketplace with the fulfillment model described accurately (Amazon handles printing/shipping/service, seller gets a royalty split), and the sub-niche strategy is sound, standard print-on-demand advice for reducing competition. No specific personal revenue figures for this exact stream are given in this segment.

name: Faceless ghostwriting service
cost: None to low startup cost
what: Writing books, newsletters, LinkedIn posts, or email sequences under someone else's name for pay, with the client taking public credit, optionally speeding up drafting with AI tools.
pitch: Cost of entry is just writing ability plus AI tools. The presenter suggests starting with nonfiction or short-form work, which is faster to produce than fiction, noting a full 10,000-word nonfiction book commonly starts around $500 with rates climbing as you gain experience and a track record.
best: Someone who already writes competently and doesn't need public credit for the work to feel worthwhile; fiction specialists should expect substantially more effort than nonfiction ghostwriting.
truth: The presenter promotes his own paid AI writing tool partway through this segment, so the ease-of-use framing should be weighed against that incentive. The $500-for-a-10k-word-book figure is a typical starting rate, not a guarantee, and actual freelance listings vary widely by niche.

name: Upwork freelancing with AI-assisted proposals and automation delivery
cost: Very low startup cost (free Upwork account; optional AI subscription)
what: Create an Upwork profile and apply to jobs (particularly AI automation and workflow-building jobs using tools like N8N), using an AI tool (Gemini) to draft tailored proposals from your background and the specific job post, and to help write the actual automation code or copy being delivered.
pitch: The presenter says this is how he personally landed his first freelance income, eventually making over $3,000 on the platform with a 100% job success rate and a top-rated badge. He frames Upwork's advantage as reaching buyers who already know they have a problem and are looking for a solution (versus needing to convince a stranger they have a problem at all), and describes using Gemini to draft N8N automation code for clients' workflow requests.
best: Someone with some existing skill (automation, copywriting, or a technical background) willing to start with small jobs to build a track record, comfortable using AI tools to speed up both the pitch and the delivery.
truth: Upwork freelancing is a genuinely low-barrier way to get a first paying client, and AI-assisted proposals/delivery is a real time-saver, but the video also shows plenty of very low-budget job postings ($5-20) alongside a few outlier freelancers earning six figures — most income on the platform sits well below those outlier examples, and building a track record from zero still takes real time and effort.

name: Shopify store creation as a service using Claude, Build Your Store, and AutoDS
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Build ready-to-launch Shopify stores for dropshippers, local businesses, and beginner e-commerce sellers using buildyourstore.ai to generate the store's technical foundation (theme, pages, product structure, policies), then use Claude as a branding and improvement layer to rewrite the copy, product pages, and FAQ so the store feels custom rather than generic.
pitch: The presenter is specific that Claude alone shouldn't be used as the full store builder, since it tends to produce generic layouts and code without the real setup work (themes, shipping policies, product structures) a functioning store needs, whereas buildyourstore.ai handles that foundation in minutes and integrates directly with AutoDS for automatically importing trending, pre-vetted products. The offer can be tailored by customer type, "a one-product dropshipping store" for dropshippers, "a merch store" for creators, or "a starter Shopify store" for total beginners.
best: Someone comfortable stacking a few specific tools together (a store-builder platform, Claude for copy, a product-sourcing app) rather than building everything from scratch, and willing to reach out to businesses directly or list the service on Fiverr.
truth: The specific tool recommended, buildyourstore.ai, comes bundled with a promotional Shopify deal ($1/month for 3 months) that the presenter's own channel appears to benefit from promoting. The underlying two-layer approach, a purpose-built store tool for the technical foundation plus Claude for the branding layer on top, is a reasonable and independently testable structure regardless of which specific store-builder is used.

name: Working as a remote audio/video transcriber
cost: Free (sign up and pass a typing/accuracy test)
what: Turn audio and video into text for companies like Rev, GoTranscript, TranscribeMe, and Scribie, after passing a short typing/accuracy test; medical and legal transcription pays more but requires accuracy certifications.
pitch: Rev's average transcriber makes about $156/month working around 15 jobs, with top earners hitting $900-1,500/month; medical/legal transcription runs $25-40/hour. The video is explicit that pay is per audio-minute, not per hour worked, so real hourly pay depends heavily on your typing speed.
best: Someone with fast, accurate typing; the video recommends testing your own speed honestly before committing real time.
truth: Named transcription platforms and their per-minute pay structure are real and accurately described, including the honest gap between advertised and real hourly rates depending on typing speed.

name: Commercial dock and door equipment service
cost: Moderate to high startup cost (specialized tools, van)
what: Repair and maintain the dock levelers, roll-up doors, and dock seals that every warehouse and distribution center relies on to load and unload trucks, and sign accounts to quarterly preventive-maintenance contracts.
pitch: When a loading bay breaks, a warehouse can't load or unload trucks, so operators will pay premium rates for same-day emergency repair on top of standard preventive-maintenance contracts. The presenters point to the ongoing warehouse and e-commerce boom as a structural tailwind that keeps this market growing every year.
best: Someone with real electrical and hydraulic know-how, since this is effectively a skilled trade working with motors, sensors, and safety systems, not a business you can outsource entirely from day one.
truth: The presenters rank this in the middle of their list specifically because of the technical skill and safety risk involved, since it's your hands doing the diagnosing and fixing unless you eventually buy your way into an existing operation. They're clear this isn't a laptop business.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Offering tree swing installation as a add-on service, growing through local Facebook community page endorsements
cost: Low (materials for the swing itself run roughly $500-700 per job, often paid by the customer)
what: Offer tree swing installation, either as a standalone service or as an add-on to an existing tree-care/climbing business, and grow it by asking happy customers to post a photo and endorsement on their local Facebook community page (which the presenter says spreads unusually well for this specific service); also consider partnering directly with online tree-swing retailers who need a referral network of local installers for the swings they sell.
pitch: The presenter cites a real tree-climbing company that has done over 500 tree swing installations (worth $250,000+ at the low end of the $500-700 price range) as a side offering to their main business, with a waitlist of over 50 people despite it not being their primary focus.
best: Someone with (or able to build a relationship with) tree-climbing/arborist skills, comfortable using local Facebook groups for word-of-mouth marketing.
truth: This is a real, verifiable company (Piedmont Tree Climbing) with the installation volume and waitlist as described. The Facebook-endorsement growth mechanic and swing-retailer partnership idea are the presenter's own suggested strategies, not independently demonstrated results.

name: Compressing free sawmill sawdust into wood pellets and selling them as heating fuel or livestock feed pellets
cost: Moderate (machine price not stated in this segment; produces 80-100kg/hour)
what: Buy a pellet mill and collect sawdust, dry leaves, rice husks, or straw for free or nearly free from sawmills (who otherwise burn it just to get rid of it), compress it into 4-12mm pellets with no glue or chemicals needed, and sell the pellets as fuel to bakeries with wood-fired ovens, barbecue restaurants, mountain hotels, industrial furnaces, and households with pellet stoves; using a different die on the same machine, produce feed pellets for livestock, poultry, and cattle operations instead.
pitch: The presenter highlights that the exact same sawdust considered worthless trash locally is sold by the ton as a commercial product in other markets, arguing the only difference is whether it's been compressed into a usable form, with finished pellets described as reaching roughly $1,400 in product value from zero-cost raw material.
best: Someone near a sawmill or similar dry-waste source, willing to build relationships with both fuel buyers and potential livestock-feed buyers.
truth: Wood pellet production from sawdust waste is a real, established biomass fuel industry practice. No specific personal revenue case study is given; the $1,400 figure appears to describe cumulative product value, not a single transaction.

name: Offering self-loading mini dumper hauling for tight residential construction sites
cost: Low ($1,300-3,200 for the machine)
what: Operate a self-loading mini dumper (front loader shovel plus hydraulic dump bed on tracks or tight-turning wheels) to move dirt and gravel through narrow residential side yards, small gates, and steep slopes that full-size dump trucks and wheelbarrow crews can't handle efficiently.
pitch: Renting the machine with yourself as operator pulls $250-450/day, pitched to pool installation crews, drainage contractors, and landscaping teams doing retaining walls, since one mini dumper replaces roughly three manual laborers and cuts job time significantly.
best: Someone comfortable operating small construction equipment and willing to market directly to residential contractors doing tight-access jobs.
truth: This is a real, niche piece of specialized construction equipment addressing a genuine access problem; the day-rate figures are presented as general industry pricing, not a verified personal case study.

name: Renting student musical instruments to school band programs
cost: Moderate (a starter fleet of 10-50 used student horns runs $5,000-15,000)
what: Buy a fleet of used student-grade band instruments (flutes, clarinets, trumpets) and rent them to middle/high school band students for $20-50/month, 9-10 months a year, to a new student every school year for a decade; collect a deposit and offer a rent-to-own option to cover damage risk, and land the first customers by contacting band directors directly and showing up at instrument-fitting nights.
pitch: The video cites Music & Arts, a national chain built entirely on this model, as proof of real demand, and frames the appeal as parents not wanting to buy a $900 trumpet for a 12-year-old who might quit by March; a small fleet can generate a few hundred to over $1,000/month once established, with each instrument paying for itself in 1-2 school years.
best: Someone willing to build relationships with local school band directors and comfortable managing a rental inventory (deposits, condition tracking, cleaning) over multiple school years.
truth: Instrument rental to school band programs is a real, established model with a genuine large existing competitor validating demand. No specific personal case study or verified revenue figure is given for an independent small operator; figures are general industry ranges.

name: Mobile phlebotomy contract work
cost: Requires phlebotomy certification (moderate time/cost investment, but described as far less than most medical training paths)
what: Work as a certified mobile phlebotomist, traveling to offices, events, or homes to draw blood for medical purposes (routine testing, cancer screening events, etc.), contracting with companies that need on-site blood draw services rather than working in a fixed clinical setting.
pitch: A presenter reports making $600 in under 4 hours of work on back-to-back days, eventually quitting two other jobs to do this full-time, and describes getting paid $85/hour plus a $6 reimbursement per patient for an event-based cancer-screening blood draw project, with supply costs under $3 per patient.
best: Someone willing to get phlebotomy certification first, comfortable with medical/clinical work, and looking for a healthcare-adjacent gig with notably higher hourly pay than typical gig work.
truth: The pay rate described ($85/hour) is genuinely high for this kind of work, and unlike most items on this list, it requires real certification and skill, which raises the barrier to entry but also the pay ceiling. This isn't a same-day-start hustle — expect to invest time and some money in certification before earning anything.

name: Feeder insect breeding business selling to reptile owners
cost: Low startup cost ($150-300 for colony starter and housing)
what: Breed feeder insects (dubia roaches) for sale to reptile owners, who need a constant weekly supply for pets like bearded dragons and geckos over a decade-long lifespan, making this a genuinely recurring-demand product once a colony is established.
pitch: A dubia roach colony starter runs $45-135 depending on size, with bins, egg crates, and heat bringing total setup to $150-300. The presenter is blunt about failure modes: dubia barely breed at room temperature (one breeder wasted 6 months before realizing they lacked a heat source), colonies crash from mold in wet bins or overcrowding, and one operator lost 25% of a colony in 2 days from pesticide-contaminated feed (non-organic quinoa). He also warns that a mealworm breeder quit the business entirely after lung damage from frass dust, even while wearing a mask.
best: Someone willing to closely manage temperature, humidity, and feed quality for a live colony, and to take a genuine health precaution (proper ventilation) seriously rather than treating it as optional.
truth: The recurring-demand logic (reptile owners need feeders every week for years) is sound, but this is one of the more failure-prone ideas on the list — multiple specific ways to lose most or all of a colony are documented, plus a real respiratory health risk from insect frass dust that isn't fully solved by a basic mask.

name: Becoming an AI-focused content creator in a specific underserved niche, using AI tools to handle scripting and production
cost: Low (Claude for scripts, an AI image/video tool for thumbnails/B-roll)
what: Create content specifically about using AI/Claude for a chosen audience, using Claude to write and repurpose scripts and an AI image/video tool to generate thumbnails and motion graphics rather than needing design skills; study 3-5 existing creators in the space (breaking down their scripts, strategy, and branding with Claude) not to copy them, but to identify a specific gap or angle nobody else is covering yet.
pitch: The presenter cites a client, a former insurance sales manager with no prior AI knowledge, who reached 50,000 YouTube subscribers and over $50,000/month within 6 months while working full-time and raising three kids; he scores this 19/25 (ease 3, speed 3, validated 5, competition 3-4, long-term 5) and notes monetization through brand deals, info products/courses, and one-on-one client work, with AdSense treated as bonus income rather than the core plan.
best: Someone willing to be on camera and consistently produce content, comfortable studying competitors analytically to find a real gap rather than copying them.
truth: AI-assisted content creation tools for scripting, thumbnails, and editing are real and current, and the specific case study (a named client's follower/revenue growth) is a concrete claim, though self-reported and not independently audited. The video promotes the presenter's own free 3-day training and paid coaching.

name: Running a portable restroom rental business for construction sites and events
cost: Moderate to high (purchasing multiple portable restroom units)
what: Buy portable restroom units and rent them to construction sites, events, and fairs on a per-event or per-month basis, cleaning them on a scheduled route and collecting payment each rental cycle rather than selling anything outright.
pitch: The presenter cites the global portable restroom rental market at $20.71 billion, projected to reach $34.86 billion by 2030 per Grand View Research, framing the business's unattractiveness as precisely what keeps competition low.
best: Someone with capital to invest in multiple units and willing to manage a scheduled servicing/cleaning route.
truth: Portable restroom rental is a real, established equipment-rental business model with genuine recurring demand from construction and events, and the cited market-size figures come from a named third-party research source. No specific per-unit or per-operator revenue example is given in this segment.

name: Lawn care and mowing route
cost: Low startup cost (one mower to start)
what: Build a residential lawn mowing and basic yard maintenance route, starting with one mower and expanding customer by customer within a tight geographic area to keep drive time low and route density high.
pitch: Zaback cites the U.S. lawn care and landscaping industry at $184 billion in 2025 across 650,000 companies, none of which controls more than 5% of the market, meaning there's no dominant national brand cornering any given neighborhood. He notes the average U.S. household spends about $600 a year on lawn care, and that doing eight to ten lawns a day can generate $400 to $750 in daily revenue solo.
best: Someone willing to start small (one mower, one tight route) and treat this as a long, proven, unglamorous path rather than a fast or novel one, since Zaback frames it as one of the least flashy but most consistently reliable ideas on the list.
truth: The revenue figures are Zaback's general framework based on typical job counts and pricing rather than one specific named case study, unlike some of the other ideas in this video. The market fragmentation statistic (no company over 5% share) is a real, checkable structural fact about the industry that supports the claim of low competitive barriers, regardless of any individual operator's specific results.

name: Short-form video clipping service using Opus Clip
cost: Very low startup cost (Opus Clip subscription)
what: Take a creator's or business's existing long-form video content and use the AI tool Opus Clip to automatically generate 10 to 20 short vertical clips for TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts, then lightly edit and caption the best ones before delivering them to the client.
pitch: Hamilton frames the pricing specifically around undercutting manual editors: professional editors who clip content by hand typically charge $50 to $80 per clip, so charging $10 to $20 per clip, or a flat bundle like $300 a month for around 30 clips across four videos, still feels like a bargain to the client while paying you roughly $100 an hour for the actual editing time involved. The differentiator she stresses is not just running the AI tool and handing over raw output, but going back into Opus Clip's editing tools to adjust captions and trim clips so they're genuinely polished before delivery.
best: Someone with an eye for what makes a short clip watchable who's willing to do a bit of manual polish on top of the AI-generated output, rather than just delivering the raw automated clips.
truth: Hamilton pays someone else to do a version of this for her own content, which is a real, if secondhand, validation that people pay for this service. The specific dollar figures ($10-20/clip, $300/month bundle, roughly $100/hour in time) are her own suggested pricing framework, not a documented case study of someone else successfully charging these rates.

name: AI-personalized, trigger-based sales prospecting service
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Feed Claude a prospect and a specific trigger event, a funding round, a new hire, a relevant post, and have it draft a short, non-pitchy outreach message that references the trigger directly, so a sales team spends less time hunting for leads and writing near-identical cold messages and more time on actual conversations.
pitch: Hawksworth's pitch is that this doesn't replace a sales team, it removes the boring research and first-draft-writing work that eats their week, while keeping the human conversation, which he argues is what actually closes deals, intact. He suggests charging around £1,500 to set the system up and £750 a month to keep it running and the CRM organized.
best: Someone selling into businesses that already have a sales team or process in place and just need the research and outreach-drafting work taken off their plate, rather than businesses with no sales process at all.
truth: The pricing figures (£1,500 setup, £750/month) are the presenter's own suggested starting points, not documented client outcomes. This kind of trigger-based, one-prospect-at-a-time personalization is a specific tactic within the broader AI-powered sales space that shows up across a lot of WAH creator content, and the underlying mechanic, feeding Claude a single prospect and trigger, is simple enough to test yourself before paying for training on it.

name: AI chatbots for support and sales
cost: Low startup cost
what: Build support or sales chatbots for businesses to handle repetitive customer questions on their website or messaging channels.
pitch: A lower-complexity entry point into AI services compared to voice agents or full automation systems, since chatbot-building tools have become fairly plug-and-play.
best: Someone looking for the simplest, fastest entry point into selling AI tools to businesses, even if it means lower differentiation.
truth: Gadzhi is fairly blunt here: he considers this overhyped and easy to commoditize, meaning a lot of people offer a very similar product, which puts downward pressure on what you can charge.

name: White-label SaaS reseller for local business niches (GoHighLevel)
cost: Low startup cost (~$497/month software fee, plus ad spend)
found: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
what: You white-label GoHighLevel's all-in-one marketing and CRM software and resell it to local business niches (event rental companies, med spas, gyms, dentists, roofers, and similar), charging a monthly software fee while your own reseller cost stays fixed at $497 a month regardless of how many clients you have.
pitch: Koerner reverse-engineers real competitors using GoHighLevel's own public "SaaSpreneur" awards page, which shows which resellers have crossed 100, 500, or 1,000+ paying customers, then walks through a five-tool toolkit: the pricing page, the Wayback Machine, the Meta Ads Library, builtwith.com, and LinkedIn, to estimate a competitor's real revenue, ad spend, and team size. He demonstrates the model live by building a "missed call text back" tool for a roofing business in a few minutes inside GoHighLevel, showing how a small wedge product can turn into a broader retainer relationship.
best: Someone comfortable with sales and marketing research who's willing to pick one underserved local-business niche and specialize in it, rather than trying to serve every industry at once.
truth: Koerner discloses upfront that he's a GoHighLevel affiliate and earns a commission if viewers sign up through his link, worth keeping in mind given how enthusiastically the software is framed. All of the specific revenue estimates for the example businesses are his own "back of a napkin" math based on public award tiers and pricing pages, not verified financials, a reasonable estimate but not an audited number. The reverse-engineering toolkit itself is genuinely useful and independently verifiable regardless of how accurate any single revenue guess turns out to be.

name: Building a vending machine route
cost: Low to moderate startup cost (used machines can be bought cheaply, or financed)
what: Place and maintain vending machines in local businesses (offices, warehouses, workshops), splitting a percentage of revenue with the location owner in exchange for the convenience of on-site food or drinks with no effort on their part.
pitch: Tilbury's illustrative example is a young operator who approached a workshop with an old, unprofitable coffee machine and offered to install three new machines at no cost to the business owner, handling all maintenance and restocking himself, in exchange for a 15% cut of revenue. That operator scaled to machines across the state, all generating passive income once installed. Used vending machines are widely available cheaply, and can be financed and paid off from the route's own profits.
best: Someone comfortable with the upfront legwork of finding good locations and negotiating placement deals, who's willing to handle restocking and maintenance (or eventually hire someone to) rather than someone looking for something entirely hands-off from day one.
truth: The industry-level figure cited (Selecta reporting over $1 billion in 2021 sales, up 3% year over year) is a real, checkable industry data point distinct from the personal anecdote about the young operator, which is presented as a story Tilbury witnessed rather than a verified case study with real numbers attached. The core advice, that success depends on finding the right locations and the right product mix for each one, is genuinely the hard part of this business, not a minor detail.

name: Placing coin-operated motorcycle helmet cleaning vending machines at motorcycle-traffic locations
cost: Moderate ($1,691 for the machine)
what: Place a coin-slot vending machine that cleans, UV/ozone-disinfects, heats (40-60°C), and defogs motorcycle helmet visors, at locations with existing motorcycle foot traffic: dealerships, motorcycle parking lots, car washes, repair shops; the machine is cloud-controlled and remotely monitored so you can track sales and service needs across multiple locations without being physically present.
pitch: The presenter argues helmets are almost never washed (can't go in a washing machine, easy to damage by hand) despite being worn sweaty for hours daily, and frames the customer base as permanently growing since every new motorcycle sold means one more helmet that will eventually need cleaning.
best: Someone comfortable managing multiple remote vending locations rather than a single physical storefront.
truth: Coin-operated, cloud-monitored vending equipment for niche cleaning needs is a real, established small-business model. No specific revenue figures given.

name: Pad printing business for branding curved products
cost: Low startup cost (about $650-950 for a desktop pad printing machine)
what: Use a pad printing machine (which transfers ink from an engraved plate via a flexible silicone pad) to brand curved or uneven objects that flat presses can't handle — pens, bottle caps, tool handles, plastic cases — selling primarily to local businesses that need only 50-100 branded pieces, a quantity too small for large suppliers who prefer orders in the thousands.
pitch: A beginner setup (a single-color desktop machine, printing plates, silicone pads, suitable inks, cleaning supplies, product fixtures, blank test items) costs $650-950. The presenter warns that consistency is the hard part — each product may need a different plate, pad, ink, and fixture, and an item that shifts during printing produces a crooked or blurred logo.
best: Someone comfortable with a technical, fixture-dependent process who wants to fill the specific gap between individual custom orders and factory-scale bulk branding runs.
truth: The market gap identified (large suppliers won't touch small orders of 50-100 curved items) is genuine and specific, which is more defensible than a generic "branded promotional products" business — but the per-product setup complexity (different plate/pad/ink combinations) means this isn't a simple one-machine-fits-all operation.

name: Neocaridina shrimp breeding business selling to local fish stores
cost: Low startup cost (about $150-300 for a single-tank starter setup with livestock)
what: Breed Neocaridina shrimp (a popular, colorful freshwater aquarium species) in a home tank setup, selling to local fish stores as a consistent wholesale buyer and to aquarium clubs/online sales at higher per-unit prices but lower volume.
pitch: A 10-gallon setup with starter livestock runs $150-250, or a 20-gallon all-in-one kit for $250-300. Low-grade shrimp sell $1-3 each, mid-grade $3-5, high-grade $5-8, and breeding females $8-15. The presenter frames this explicitly as supplemental income that compounds slowly, not fast money, and warns that failing to cull low-grade offspring causes color quality to degrade across generations, drifting an entire colony back to plain wild-type coloring (and losing the price point) within a year.
best: Someone with patience for a slow-building, low-maintenance supplemental income stream, who's willing to actively cull a colony to maintain color quality rather than letting it breed freely.
truth: The presenter is upfront that this is slow supplemental income, not a primary income replacement, which is a more honest framing than most livestock-breeding side hustle content — the ongoing culling discipline required to maintain value is a real, easy-to-skip maintenance task that determines whether the business stays profitable.

name: Equipment rental business
cost: Often $50,000 to $100,000 or more per piece of equipment
what: Buy commercial or industrial equipment, like compressors, and rent it out to businesses that need it temporarily rather than owning it themselves.
pitch: Presented as tax-efficient, since equipment can typically be fully depreciated, alongside steady rental income.
best: Someone with real capital to deploy and existing relationships or knowledge in a specific trade or industry.
truth: Grounded in the presenter's own real business experience with equipment needs, which lends some credibility. This requires meaningful capital and local delivery logistics, not a low-cost entry point.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Running a floor mat and work uniform exchange route for offices and restaurants
cost: Moderate (vehicle and initial mat/uniform inventory)
what: Run a route where a driver visits offices and restaurants every two weeks, swapping dirty floor mats and work uniforms for clean ones, billed as a recurring B2B service contract.
pitch: The presenter cites Cintas, a $9.6 billion company built on exactly this simple exchange model, controlling nearly a third of a $20+ billion industry, framing it as proof that a genuinely boring, repeatable route business can scale enormously without any unique invention.
best: Someone comfortable with a driving/logistics route business and building recurring B2B service contracts.
