what: Build a modern landing page for a local business, a restaurant, gym, dentist, or estate agent with an old or confusing site, by describing the business to an AI website builder (the video uses Framer, alongside Claude and Claude Code), then doing the human work of sharpening the message and call to action.
pitch: Hawksworth is explicit that AI removes most of the technical build time, generating a full landing page live in the video, but argues the real value was never the code, it's understanding who the customer is, what the offer is, and what's stopping them from buying, which is still work a person has to do. He suggests charging around £1,500 per page, plus ongoing support to keep it maintained.
best: Someone with a decent eye for what makes a page convert, a clear offer, a strong call to action, who's willing to do that judgment work on top of what the AI generates, rather than just shipping the AI's first draft.
truth: The £1,500 price point is the presenter's own suggestion rather than a documented sale. This is a similar underlying mechanic to other AI-website-building content in this space, with Framer as the specific tool of choice here, worth trying a couple of AI website builders yourself to see which workflow you prefer before committing to one.

name: AI-assisted video editing for creators and brands
cost: Low startup cost
what: Offer video editing services to creators and brands, using AI tools to speed up cuts, captions, and repurposing footage into multiple formats.
pitch: AI has significantly lowered the skill floor for competent video editing, making this an accessible service to offer even without a traditional editing background.
best: Someone looking for a straightforward, in-demand service with a short learning curve.
truth: Because the tools have made this easy to learn, it's also easy to copy, Gadzhi frames it plainly as a race to the bottom on pricing unless you find a way to specialize or work with higher-value clients.

name: Landing Upwork retainer clients in a skill you don't have, using AI to fake and then actually deliver the competency
cost: Very low (a ChatGPT/Claude subscription, an Upwork account, Loom for video pitches)
found: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
what: Apply to Upwork jobs in a skill you don't actually have (e.g. SEO) by slightly tilting away from the most saturated keyword phrasing, record a short (2-3 minute) unedited Loom video pitching how you'd approach the client's problem using an AI-built workflow, win the retainer, then actually deliver the work by learning the skill just-in-time with AI tools (Claude Code for automation build-out), and increase the retainer price once results are proven by expanding scope.
pitch: The interview subject describes going from severe poverty to a $3,000/month Upwork retainer (later raised to $5,500/month with the same client) after just 7 job applications and zero prior SEO experience, using ChatGPT to build the actual automation and a confident, unedited Loom pitch video to win trust. She expanded into content creation, a paid community, sponsorships, and a self-built app as additional income layers once inbound interest picked up from her YouTube channel.
best: Someone comfortable pitching themselves into work outside their existing skillset and willing to learn just-in-time with AI tools under real client pressure; helps to have some video-comfort for the Loom pitch step.
truth: AI genuinely lowers the bar to producing passable client deliverables fast, and Upwork niche-tilting to reduce competition is a real, sound tactic. Most of this video is the subject's personal mindset framing and multiple loosely-connected income streams rather than a single step-by-step process, and her reported income figures and timeline are self-reported and not independently verified — treat this as one real example of the method rather than a guaranteed outcome.

name: Full brand identity design service
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Design a business's complete visual identity (logo, color palette, typography, imagery style) as a full package rather than a single deliverable like a logo, aimed at businesses that want to look immediately recognizable and trustworthy to customers.
pitch: Tilbury cites Jack Watson, who went from a negative bank balance to his first $20,000 month within six months of specializing in this. The pitch leans on a clear market gap: there are many designers charging around $50 for a quick logo, but few offering the complete, cohesive package that makes a brand feel genuinely professional, which is why brand identity is positioned as a premium, underserved tier of graphic design. As evidence of real market size, the video cites the global brand identity market valued at over $9.5 billion in 2024, projected to reach $40 billion by 2032, and a real example of the UK government reportedly spending roughly $650,000 on a single logo redesign.
best: Someone with genuine visual design skill and taste who's willing to develop a full-package offering rather than staying at the cheaper, more commoditized single-logo tier of the market.
truth: The market-size figures ($9.5 billion in 2024, projected $40 billion by 2032) and the government logo redesign cost are specific, checkable claims, though the market-size numbers' original source isn't named in the video. The Jack Watson case study, like the others in this video, is featured because he's an instructor on the presenter's own paid course platform, worth factoring in when weighing how the results are framed. The underlying market gap described (cheap single-logo work vs. a full cohesive identity package) is a genuine, recognizable distinction in the design industry, independent of any specific case study's numbers.

name: Manufacturing braided rope for both industrial buyers and the higher-margin home decor/craft market
cost: High ($6,000 for the machine)
what: Buy a braiding machine (braids 3, 4, or 6 strands simultaneously, producing rope from 3mm cord to 60mm mooring rope by changing configuration) and sell into two distinct markets with the same equipment: industrial/utility buyers (construction, agriculture, fishing, moving/trucking companies, gyms) who buy by the kilogram and compare on price, and the home decor/craft market (colored cotton rope for macrame, plant hangers, woven furniture) sold to artisans and craft stores at considerably higher margins.
pitch: The presenter frames the craft/decor market as the more profitable of the two, since those buyers aren't comparing prices down to the penny the way industrial bulk buyers do, while both markets represent businesses that structurally can't operate without rope, not one-time impulse customers.
best: Someone willing to serve both a price-sensitive industrial market and a higher-margin craft/decor market with the same core equipment.
truth: Braided rope manufacturing is a real, established industrial process, and the industrial-vs-craft margin distinction described is sound, plausible market segmentation. No specific revenue figures given.

name: Producing personalized and branded products for businesses and events using a small laser engraving machine
cost: Moderate for the list (average starter machine price around $450, plus safety/ventilation gear, under $1,000)
what: Use a small laser engraving machine to mark or cut designs onto wood, leather, acrylic, cardboard, paper, bamboo, or coated metals, focusing on one niche (gifts, business branding, wedding items, or packaging accessories) rather than trying to sell everything to everyone, producing small custom batches for businesses and events that need volumes too small for a factory but too large to do one at a time.
pitch: Presented as a machine whose real opportunity only becomes clear once you understand where a laser engraver fits between mass factories and single-item hobbyists; the presenter recommends choosing one niche first, then approaching buyers who already need custom work with samples.
best: Someone willing to pick a specific niche and build a sample portfolio to approach relevant local buyers, rather than selling generic engraved items broadly.
truth: Laser engraving for small-batch personalization and branding is a real, established micro-manufacturing niche, and the advice to niche down rather than sell everything is sound. No specific revenue example is given; ventilation and safety equipment are a genuine real requirement, not optional.

name: Processing and bundling firewood for retail sale near gas stations and campgrounds
cost: Moderate ($2,000-20,000 depending on splitter and truck)
what: Source logs (ideally through free/cheap relationships with arborists and loggers rather than buying truckloads), split and bundle firewood, and sell bundles at retail locations like gas stations near campgrounds, or seasoned cords directly to homeowners with fireplaces; margin depends heavily on sourcing cost, not just sale price.
pitch: The video cites one documented operator earning around $8,000/month, with a University Extension budget showing about $48 profit per cord (roughly $337 per 7-cord truckload) for a lean two-person crew buying logs wholesale, and notes seasoned hardwood sells for $250-350/cord in colder markets.
best: Someone with access to a truck and wood-splitting equipment, and ideally relationships with arborists/loggers for cheap or free log sourcing to protect margin.
truth: Firewood processing and retail bundling is a real, established seasonal business, and the University Extension cost breakdown cited gives genuine third-party grounding to the margin figures. This is explicitly seasonal (winter-concentrated) income, which the video is upfront about.

name: Running a recurring asphalt crack-sealing maintenance service for commercial parking lots
cost: Low ($600-1,200 for an entry-level commercial unit)
what: Use an asphalt crack-sealing machine (heats rubberized sealant to over 300°F and applies it via spray wand) to seal cracks in commercial parking lots and driveways before water/ice damage turns them into expensive potholes, then lock in recurring seasonal (typically spring) maintenance contracts with the same properties.
pitch: Charges $5-10 per linear meter; a strip mall lot with 500 meters of cracking is a $2,500-5,000 payday for one afternoon of work, pitched to commercial property managers, logistics hub operators, and HOA boards as protection against a future $50,000 repaving bill.
best: Someone comfortable pitching recurring maintenance contracts to property managers and HOA boards, not just one-off jobs.
truth: Asphalt crack sealing is a real, well-established preventive-maintenance trade, and the recurring-contract framing (annual retainer with property managers) reflects how this service is genuinely often sold. Pricing figures are general industry ranges.

name: Media-kit sponsorships and done-for-you agency services layered on a content site
cost: Low incremental cost once a site or channel already has traffic — a monetization add-on rather than a standalone startup
what: Once a content site or channel has real traffic or rankings, build a simple media kit and sell sponsorship inventory directly to brands (sponsored articles, ad reads, newsletter sends, or flat fees for guaranteed placement in a ranking article), and additionally pitch brands done-for-you services like running their PPC campaigns or content/SEO strategy for a monthly retainer.
pitch: The argument is to think of yourself as a media company rather than a small affiliate blog, opening a higher-margin revenue layer not tied to affiliate conversion rates or algorithm swings, since a brand already benefiting from your rankings is in a weak negotiating position.
best: Creators or bloggers who already have ranking content or an existing audience and are comfortable with direct B2B outreach, pitching, and negotiation.
truth: The underlying mechanic (brands paying flat fees or retainers for placement) is plausible and consistent with real media/affiliate negotiations, though the cited figures are unverified anecdotes. The pitch is somewhat oversold in its own framing — despite language suggesting this works 'even with no traffic,' the entire pitch to brands depends on already having an audience or ranking asset to sell against, making this a monetization upgrade for an existing site rather than an independent starting business.

name: Circular knitting machine for beanies, scarves, and blankets
cost: $80-165 for the machine
what: A hand-crank circular knitting machine that produces beanies, scarves, leg warmers, and blankets in minutes rather than the days or weeks hand-knitting would take, requiring no actual knitting skill, just turning a handle.
pitch: A beanie costs roughly $2 in yarn to produce and sells for $10-25, and the video specifically highlights that knitted items carry a strong perceived value, buyers assume "handmade" means slow, skilled, artisan work, and price accordingly, regardless of how quickly the machine actually produced it. Demand is seasonal but predictable, spiking heavily as winter approaches.
best: Someone looking for a low-cost entry into the handmade goods market (Etsy, craft fairs, boutiques) without needing to actually learn to knit.
truth: The cost and price figures given are broadly consistent with what's publicly available for circular knitting machines and finished knitted goods. No named operator or verified sales record backs the specific numbers, so treat the income potential as illustrative rather than a demonstrated case study.

name: Building simple niche management software that solves one operational problem for a specific small-business trade
cost: Low to moderate (development time/cost, potentially AI-assisted)
what: Build simple, unglamorous management software targeting one specific operational problem for a specific trade (e.g. appointment scheduling for electricians, inventory systems for small shops), rather than attempting to build a broadly innovative app; the software doesn't need to be brilliant, it just needs to take one annoying, recurring task off a business owner's plate that they're already willing to pay to avoid doing themselves.
pitch: The presenter argues a small business owner already paying $100/month for a mediocre existing tool isn't looking for innovation, they're looking for the problem to disappear, so software that simply and reliably does that wins a recurring customer without competing against big tech for attention or funding.
best: Someone with (or willing to learn, potentially with AI assistance) basic software development skills, willing to deeply understand one specific trade's operational pain points.
truth: Narrow, vertical-specific small-business software is a real, well-documented category (often called 'boring SaaS') with a genuine track record of profitable, low-competition niches, and the framing (solve one annoying task, not build something innovative) reflects widely-cited advice from successful vertical-software founders. No specific revenue example is given in this segment.

name: Becoming an online notary for remote document signings
cost: Low (notary course and state licensing/bonding fees; process took about a week per the presenter)
what: Become licensed as a notary (a short course plus a court swearing-in in the presenter's state) and perform notarizations, most of which now happen online through dedicated apps/platforms, allowing full-time or part-time remote work handling document signings and oaths.
pitch: The presenter, who has done this herself, shows real footage of a fast online signing and describes ongoing notification requests for work years after getting licensed, rating it 4/5 for ease and 3/5 for speed to first income since it can take time to find a platform that supplies consistent work.
best: Someone willing to complete their state's notary licensing process and comfortable conducting brief, professional video-call signings.
truth: Online/remote notarization is a real, legitimate, licensed profession with genuine platforms connecting notaries to signing work, and the presenter speaks from firsthand ongoing experience rather than a one-time attempt. Licensing requirements, costs, and the legality of remote online notarization vary by state, which isn't detailed in this segment.

name: Custom photo jigsaw puzzle business
cost: Moderate startup cost (a printer or press, puzzle blanks or board, a die or laser cutter, and protective packaging)
what: Convert customer-submitted photos into jigsaw puzzles by sublimation printing onto puzzle blanks or printing onto board and die/laser-cutting, offered in sizes from quick 48-piece gifts to 500-piece challenges, delivered as a boxed puzzle featuring the customer's own image (family, wedding, pet, vacation photos).
pitch: Sell through Etsy, a personal site, and gift shops, with seasonal bundles (holiday photos, baby's-first-year sets) to boost volume and corporate clients using branded puzzles for events — the presenter frames the combination of personalization, play, and keepsake value as support for premium pricing and repeat gifting.
best: Someone comfortable with print production equipment (sublimation or laser cutting) and interested in a seasonal, gift-occasion-driven sales pattern.
truth: Photo puzzles are an established, proven personalized-gift category with genuine repeat-purchase potential around recurring occasions (holidays, weddings, births). Print/cut equipment represents a real upfront cost compared to some other items on this list, and quality consistency (image resolution, cut precision) directly affects both customer satisfaction and repeat business.

name: Hand-painting custom signs and party banners as an alternative to vinyl printing
cost: Very low for the banner version (under $200 for paint, brushes, a projector for tracing designs, and Canva for layout); storefront sign painting requires more skill investment but similar low material cost
what: Hand-paint lettering, logos, or artwork instead of using vinyl printing, either as birthday/bachelorette/sweet-16 paper banners (traced with a projector from a Canva design, sold for $60-$120 each, taking under an hour per banner) or, at a more skilled level, as storefront and mural signage sold directly to businesses for hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars.
pitch: The presenter cites two examples: Alex Slabik, who built a following of nearly 600,000 selling hand-painted party banners via Instagram/TikTok DMs with no website or ad spend, and Will Van Z, who hand-paints and gold-leaf-gilds storefront signage for restaurants and shops in New York. He frames vinyl printing's dominance as having created an opening for the hand-crafted alternative.
best: Someone with (or willing to develop) hand-lettering/painting skill, comfortable building an audience by documenting the painting process on social media to drive DM-based orders.
truth: The core observation, that hand-craftsmanship stands out against mass-produced vinyl printing and can support a real following-driven sales channel, is sound, and the banner version genuinely has a very low cost of entry. The follower-count and pricing figures come from two specific individual examples rather than typical outcomes, and building an audience large enough to sustain consistent DM orders took real, sustained content effort, not just posting a few paintings.

name: Remote-run residential cleaning business
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Run a residential house-cleaning business without doing any of the cleaning yourself. Hire independent cleaners who already own their own supplies and vehicles, handle the marketing, scheduling, and customer relationships, and split revenue roughly 50/50 with the cleaner on every job.
pitch: The presenters rank this their overall number-one pick because it's a large, fragmented home-services market with no dominant national brand, and roughly one in three one-time cleanings converts into a recurring client, building compounding revenue instead of starting from zero every month. Using a rough example, a $350 first-time deep clean split 50/50 with the cleaner, scaled to around 25 to 30 recurring clients, gets to roughly $10,000 a month in revenue with no employees on payroll and minimal ongoing labor from the owner.
best: Someone willing to build the business around recruiting and managing independent cleaners from day one, rather than doing cleanings themselves to save money early on, which the presenters call the single most common way people sabotage this model.
truth: The presenters are explicit that this is the business they'd start themselves from zero, and flag a real failure pattern: people who fail at this almost always fail the same way, by getting personally attached to doing the cleaning and building limiting beliefs around recruiting cleaners instead of stepping into an owner role early. They also promote a paid mentorship program at the end with a stated revenue and client guarantee, worth knowing given the number of specific client success figures cited throughout the video.

name: Building an entire mobile business around window and door screen repair specifically
cost: Low (basic screen-repair materials and tools; a mobile service vehicle)
what: Offer mobile, on-site repair of window screens, retractable door screens, and sliding door screens as a standalone specialty (not a general handyman service), traveling to customers' homes rather than requiring drop-off; build a business identity entirely around this one narrow service.
pitch: The presenter found a real company (Screen Mobile) built entirely around this niche, and cites keyword data showing 'window screen repair' gets 5,400 monthly searches at a 0/100 difficulty score and 'window screen repair near me' gets 7,800 searches, also at 0/100 difficulty, with little existing dedicated content competing for either term.
best: Someone comfortable with basic screen-repair skills and a mobile, on-the-road service model.
truth: This is a real, verifiable company operating as described, and the cited keyword-volume/difficulty figures come from a named third-party SEO tool. No specific revenue figures are given for this particular business.

name: Turning free used cardboard into flexible protective packaging mesh, sold or applied on-site as a bubble-wrap alternative
cost: Low ($698 for the machine)
what: Buy a cardboard perforating machine (small, desk-sized, 150W power draw) that feeds in any used cardboard box and perforates/stretches it into a flexible cushioned mesh that absorbs impact similarly to bubble wrap, then sell the protective mesh by the meter to e-commerce businesses and logistics companies, or offer an on-site service where you process their own accumulated cardboard directly.
pitch: The presenter frames this as solving a problem online sellers are actively asking about — cheap, plastic-free protective packaging — using free raw material (cardboard is endlessly available from supermarkets and warehouses) to meet real, current demand from e-commerce businesses wanting to drop plastic packaging.
best: Someone comfortable pitching e-commerce/logistics businesses on either a product (packaging mesh) or an on-site processing service.
truth: This is a real, current small-manufacturing niche responding to a genuine e-commerce demand for plastic-free packaging alternatives. No specific personal revenue figures are given.

name: Supplying mini tart and pie shells to bakeries and caterers using a shell-forming machine, rather than selling desserts directly
cost: Moderate for the list (average starter machine price around $650, one of the more expensive, but plannable under $1,000)
what: Use a tartlet/mini pie shell forming machine to press dough into consistent, uniform tart or pie shells, then sell the empty shells wholesale to bakeries, cafes, catering kitchens, dessert shops, and event suppliers who want to sell finished desserts but don't want staff time spent hand-shaping shells, rather than building your own retail dessert brand.
pitch: Presented as an unglamorous machine most beginners skip, with the actual opportunity being becoming the boring, reliable B2B supplier behind bakeries rather than competing with them directly for retail customers.
best: Someone comfortable approaching bakeries and catering businesses directly to become a reliable wholesale supplier, rather than building a consumer-facing dessert brand.
truth: Wholesale supply of semi-finished baked components to bakeries and caterers is a real, established B2B food-industry practice. No specific revenue example is given; food-safety/hygiene compliance requirements for wholesale food supply will apply and vary by location.

name: Window cleaning business started lean and scaled through owner-built systems
cost: Very low startup cost (a squeegee, bucket, and soap to start)
what: Start a window cleaning business with minimal equipment, personally doing the cleaning work in the early stages to learn the business's actual pain points firsthand, then use that hands-on experience to build the systems and processes needed to scale the business well beyond a one-person operation.
pitch: Heacock cites a business owner, John, who started with just a squeegee, bucket, and soap cleaning windows for a single bank, and now runs a window cleaning business doing $10 million in annual revenue at a 40% net margin, or about $4 million a year in profit. Heacock frames doing the labor yourself early on as valuable specifically because it teaches you the business's real pain points before you try to build systems to solve them at scale.
best: Someone willing to do the physical labor themselves in the early stages of the business, viewing that hands-on period as market research for building scalable systems later rather than something to avoid.
truth: The lean-start-then-systematize approach is sound, practical business advice that applies well beyond window cleaning specifically. The $10 million/40% margin outcome represents a mature, fully-scaled operation with a large team, not a starting point — the presenter is clear that the real lesson is in the sequencing (labor first, systems second), not in window cleaning being a special path to that scale.

name: Running a grease trap pumping service that gets paid by the restaurant and again by a biofuel buyer
cost: Moderate to high (pump truck and equipment)
what: Pump out commercial kitchens' underground grease traps on the health-code-mandated schedule (every 1-3 months), getting paid by the restaurant for the removal service, then resell the collected used grease to biofuel producers who turn it into renewable diesel, getting paid a second time on the same material.
pitch: The presenter cites one waste company that documented recovering nearly 300 tons of used grease over 3 years, generating over $100,000 in rebates on top of what they were already being paid to remove it — a genuine double-revenue mechanic on the same collected material.
best: Someone comfortable with pump-truck route work and willing to build relationships with biofuel buyers for the resale side.
truth: Grease trap pumping is a real, health-code-mandated recurring service, and grease-to-biofuel resale is a real, established secondary market; the cited case study figures (300 tons, $100K in rebates) are attributed to one specific company, not independently verified.

name: Running a small lavender or you-pick flower farm combining product sales with visitor days
cost: Moderate to high ($10,000-50,000 depending on acreage, for land prep, plant stock, irrigation, and a small retail setup)
what: Plant and grow a small lavender (or similar flower) field, treating it as an agritourism business first rather than pure farming: charge visitors a small entry fee for you-pick bouquet days, run small workshops, and sell bundled bouquets and lavender oil to soap makers and gift shops, generating income while the field matures toward full harvest productivity over 2-3 years.
pitch: The video cites operators reporting $300-2,000/month in season blending product sales with visitor days, and notes the lavender oil market is projected to grow near 7%/year over the next decade; the honest caveat is that full bloom productivity takes 2-3 years, which the agritourism-first approach is meant to bridge.
best: Someone with land access and patience for a multi-year ramp, willing to run visitor-facing events (workshops, pick days) rather than waiting for wholesale oil contracts alone.
truth: Lavender/agritourism farming is a real, established small-farm business model, and the market-growth figure is cited from industry projections rather than the presenter's own claim. This is genuinely slower and more capital-intensive than most other items on this list, which the video is explicit about.

name: Handmade candle holder business across concrete, wood, metal, or glass
cost: Low to moderate startup cost depending on medium (molds or tooling, sanding, finishing supplies, sealers, and heat-safe testing)
what: Craft candle holders — tealight cups, taper stands, trays, candelabras — in a chosen medium (concrete mimicking stone or terrazzo, wood for warmth and engraving, metal for an industrial look, or glass), letting a seller serve the large candle-accessory market without making wax products themselves.
pitch: Build cella sets for mantels and tablescapes, stage moody styled photos with lit candles for marketing, and partner with candle makers for bundle deals; personalization (monograms, dates, motifs) is recommended to raise margins, with gift-ready boxes and felt-padded bases to elevate perceived value and reduce breakage-related returns.
best: Someone with finishing/fabrication skills in at least one medium (concrete casting, woodworking, metalwork, or glasswork) who wants to sell into the home-decor and gifting market without doing candle-making itself.
truth: This is a genuinely distinct product from candle-making itself (a separately listed business), letting a maker enter the same market from the accessories side, and partnering directly with candle makers for bundles is a sound, low-cost distribution strategy. Heat-safety testing matters for any holder meant to be used with a lit candle, and each medium has its own real skill/tooling learning curve.

name: Setting appointments for creator-led founders by messaging their own engaged followers (inbound DM setting), rather than cold outbound
cost: Very low (no special tools required beyond messaging platforms)
what: Instead of cold outbound, work exclusively with founders who already create content and have an engaged audience, finding the people who follow, engage with, and view their profile, then message those warm prospects to book a sales call or close a DM sale on the founder's behalf; only take on creators selling something genuinely high-ticket (at least $2,000), since compensation is typically a base fee plus commission.
pitch: The presenter scores this 21/25 (ease 4, speed 5, validated 5, competition 3-4, long-term 4), framing it as one of the fastest ideas on the list to land a first client (simply finding creators who post consistently but are weak at DMs) while cautioning it's a good starting point rather than a lifelong career unless scaled into a full sales agency, and cites a $1,000 base plus 5-10% commission as typical.
best: Someone comfortable with sales conversations and DM-based selling, looking for a fast-to-start opportunity rather than necessarily a long-term business.
truth: Inbound DM setting for creator-led offers is a real, active service the presenter says he personally hires for, and warm-audience outreach converting better than cold outbound is standard, sound sales logic. Pricing figures are the presenter's own stated ranges, not independently verified, and the video promotes a free companion Claude skill and paid training.

name: Specializing as an electrician in EV charging station and smart home installation for premium rates
cost: Moderate (existing electrician licensing plus specialized training/certification)
what: Take the existing electrician trade and specialize specifically in EV charging station installation and smart home systems, an emerging niche within an established profession, charging premium rates (over $250/hour cited) compared to traditional electrical work, positioning early in a growing local market before more electricians specialize in it.
pitch: The presenter frames this as the same underlying trade commanding dramatically higher rates purely through specialization timing, arguing that whoever specializes in EV charging installation first in a given area will capture premium pricing as EV adoption and home charger installation continues to grow.
best: Someone already licensed as an electrician (or willing to become one) who wants to specialize rather than remain a generalist.
truth: Electrician specialization commanding premium rates is a real, well-documented pattern in skilled trades generally, and EV charging/smart home installation is a genuinely growing, real market need as EV adoption increases. This requires an existing electrical license (a real, non-trivial barrier not detailed here), and the specific $250/hour figure is a cited rate, not a guaranteed outcome.

name: Publishing low and medium-content books (puzzle books, activity books) on Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing
cost: Very low (Amazon KDP is free to use; a template-based book creation tool for puzzle content)
what: Publish low and medium-content books through Amazon KDP's print-on-demand system (Amazon prints, ships, and handles customer service per order, paying a royalty split), focusing specifically on puzzle books, crossword books, word search books, and similar activity content rather than full-length novels, which the presenter found much harder to sell; use pre-made templates for puzzle generation rather than building content from scratch, and apply the same specific-niche thinking used for the T-shirt business.
pitch: The presenter says he originally tried this stream years earlier without much success, and only found real traction after switching strategy specifically to niche puzzle books, framing this as a valuable lesson that low-content book type (not the KDP platform itself) was the reason for his earlier failure.
best: Someone willing to niche down within the low-content book category (rather than novels) and use templated tools to speed up creation.
truth: Amazon KDP's print-on-demand model and the general distinction between the difficulty of selling novels versus low-content books are accurate and match common self-publishing knowledge. No specific revenue figures for this stream are given in this segment, only the presenter's own account of an initial failed attempt followed by later success after changing approach.

name: Short-form video content strategist for small businesses
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Help small businesses, entrepreneurs, and coaches (a local gym, a coffee shop, an estate agent) grow their audience and attention on short-form platforms by developing their content strategy, hooks, and posting approach, without needing to be the on-camera talent or creator yourself.
pitch: Tilbury cites Noah Brilley, who studied what made content go viral on TikTok as a student, tested and refined that understanding, and made over $100,000 before turning 18 helping creators, tech companies, and even banks grow their audiences this way. The pitch centers on a real behavioral statistic: the average TikTok user opens the app roughly 20 times a day and spends around 90 minutes on it daily, framed as evidence that attention itself is the scarce resource businesses are competing for, and that understanding how to capture it is a sellable skill independent of being a creator personally. A suggested pricing structure is a flat monthly fee plus a performance-based view bonus when content goes viral, which aligns incentives between strategist and client.
best: Someone with a genuine, demonstrated eye for what makes short-form content work (hooks, pacing, trends) who's more interested in strategy and analysis than being on camera themselves.
truth: The TikTok usage statistics (20 opens a day, 90 minutes average) are attributed to TikTok's own claims, a reasonable but self-reported source rather than independent audited data. The Noah Brilley case study is specific but, consistent with the other examples in this video, comes from the presenter's own paid course platform where Noah is a featured instructor. The core idea, that strategy and understanding of a platform's mechanics is a genuinely separable, sellable skill from content creation itself, is a real and increasingly common freelance service, independent of this particular case study.

name: Manufacturing mesh produce bags for agricultural harvesters and the growing reusable-bag consumer market
cost: High ($5,600 for the machine)
what: Buy a fully automatic mesh bag machine (cuts and sews simultaneously, 50 bags/minute, multi-color printing capable, produces 35-90cm wide bags) and sell into two markets: agricultural harvesters (onions, citrus, potatoes) who buy by the thousands every season since they can't sell their harvest without bags, and the growing reusable-bag consumer market driven by plastic bag bans, where a bag printed with a store's logo sells for considerably more than a plain one.
pitch: The presenter points out that produce in a supermarket is almost never loose — it's in mesh bags someone had to manufacture and sell to that store — framing the buyer as the business that packages the produce, not the shopper who takes it home, and noting agricultural buyers aren't optional customers since they literally can't sell their harvest without the bags.
best: Someone willing to serve both agricultural bulk buyers and retail-facing branded bag customers with the same equipment.
truth: Mesh bag manufacturing is a real, established agricultural packaging process, and the plastic-bag-ban-driven reusable bag trend is a genuine, current market shift. No specific revenue figures given.

name: Offering precision brick and paver cutting with a manual guillotine shear for hardscape crews
cost: Very low ($300-500 for the tool)
what: Use a manual guillotine-style stone shear (no gas, batteries, or power cords — pure mechanical lever pressure) to cut bricks, pavers, and stone blocks cleanly for hardscape crews, avoiding the dust, noise, and diamond-blade cost of a gas cutoff saw.
pitch: Charges around $100/hour or $100-150/day as a specialty add-on line item, targeting hardscape contractors building outdoor kitchens/patios, commercial landscaping crews laying paver walkways, and custom home builders doing high-end stone work.
best: Someone wanting the lowest-capital, lowest-maintenance entry on this list, comfortable doing physical lever-operated cutting work.
truth: Manual guillotine stone shears are a real, established hardscaping tool, and the clean-cut value proposition (versus a messy gas saw) is a genuine trade advantage. Pricing figures are general industry framing.

name: Freelance arbitrage: connecting people who need a service with freelancers who provide it, for a convenience fee
cost: Very low (no product or inventory needed; the business is the connection itself)
what: Identify people willing to pay for a specific service and freelancers/contractors who already perform that service, then connect the two for a convenience fee, essentially operating as a lightweight matchmaking agency; scalable by vetting and building a roster of reliable contractors, and eventually hiring people to do the work under your own brand.
pitch: The presenter calls this her highest-ceiling idea on the list because of its scalability into a full agency or even a larger company, comparing the model directly to how real estate agents and staffing brokers already operate and get paid for convenience, rating it 4/5 for ease (you're the researcher/connector, not the doer) and 3/5 for speed since vetting good contractors takes some time.
best: Someone comfortable with relationship-building and vetting service providers, willing to build trust with both clients and contractors before the model scales.
truth: Service brokering/matchmaking for a fee is a long-established, real business model (staffing agencies, real estate brokerages, and freelance-agency middlemen all operate this way), and the scalability argument is sound since the model doesn't require the operator to personally perform the service. No specific revenue example is given for this particular idea in the video; success depends on finding a service niche with a real gap between supply and demand.

name: On-demand laminating service and laminated product business
cost: Very low startup cost (a portable laminator, assorted pouches, a trimmer, and a clean work surface)
what: Offer on-demand lamination for certificates, menus, kids' art, classroom materials, and signage (pickup/drop-off for teachers, same-day service for small businesses, mobile service at parent events), plus sell your own laminated products like chore charts, meal planners, reusable worksheets, luggage tags, and dry-erase kids' placemats.
pitch: Market through school groups, libraries, parent forums, and local cafes with simple per-sheet pricing and volume discounts, and treat designed template packs (chore charts, planners) as a form of ongoing, semi-passive income once created, since the design work is done once but can be laminated and sold repeatedly.
best: Someone looking for a very low-cost, flexible service business with a fast turnaround, comfortable doing both on-location service work and designing reusable product templates.
truth: This is a genuinely low-barrier, low-risk business to test given the minimal equipment cost, and splitting revenue between a service (lamination) and a product (pre-designed laminated goods) is a sound way to diversify. Per-job margins are inherently small, so volume and repeat institutional clients (schools, offices) matter more than any single job.

name: Offering lawn leveling as a standalone service distinct from mowing or landscaping
cost: Very low to start (hand tools, a shovel and wheelbarrow, for early jobs; heavier equipment only needed once scaling to multiple daily jobs)
what: Top-dress lawns with a sand-and-compost mix to smooth out low spots and bumps until the yard is flat, marketed as a distinct service from standard mowing or landscaping, targeting homeowners, especially in newer-construction neighborhoods with poorly graded yards.
pitch: The presenter cites Brandon McLauren, who started during the pandemic after noticing the effect on his own yard, did his first $600 job with just a shovel and wheelbarrow, and scaled to about $500,000/year in lawn leveling alone, doubling revenue year over year for four years, in a home market with only two other companies offering the service.
best: Someone willing to do physically demanding manual labor initially, in a market with new-construction housing growth and little existing lawn-leveling competition.
truth: The broader lawn care market is large and well-established, and top-dressing/leveling is a genuine, recognized landscaping technique, the presenter's framing of it as an underserved standalone niche is plausible given how few dedicated providers he cites. The specific $500K/year figure is one individual's self-reported result, and this business still requires physical labor and correctly assessing whether a local market has the underserved demand the presenter describes.

name: Repackaging bulk food products into smaller retail-ready pouches using an impulse heat sealer
cost: Very low (average starter setup price around $120 for a heat sealer, digital scale, and packaging tools, one of the easiest to keep under $1,000)
what: Use an impulse heat sealer with a digital scale to repackage bulk-bought products (nuts, dates, snacks, coffee, spices, tea, dried fruit) into smaller, sealed, labeled pouches for resale, or offer packaging as a service to home food producers, starting with small test batches and simple labels before investing heavily in packaging design once real demand is confirmed.
pitch: Presented as a deceptively simple machine whose real value is turning loose, cheap-looking bulk products into sellable, professional-looking retail items; the presenter warns against over-investing in packaging design before confirming actual customer demand.
best: Someone comfortable sourcing bulk food products affordably and willing to test small batches before scaling packaging investment.
truth: Bulk repackaging and resale of food staples is a real, low-barrier micro-business model, and the 'test demand before over-investing' advice is sound, broadly applicable lean-startup guidance. No specific revenue example is given; margins depend on bulk sourcing costs relative to local retail prices.

name: Growing and selling sod to landscapers and new-construction builders
cost: High ($20,000-50,000 for a small commercial plot with irrigation and harvesting gear)
what: Grow sod on a dedicated plot and sell it by the pallet to landscapers, builders, and municipal projects tied to new-construction lawns, replanting immediately after each harvest so the same ground yields repeatedly; get a first recurring account by underpricing the local supplier on a bulk order for one subdivision buildout.
pitch: The video cites University Extension data showing roughly $8,000-12,000 in returns per acre against about $4,000 in costs per acre (so $4,000-8,000 margin per acre per cycle), with a 20-acre plot in active rotation described as real recurring monthly money through the growing season.
best: Someone with land access and patience — sod takes 9-18 months to build a harvestable root mat — and willing to build relationships with a handful of steady landscaping/building accounts rather than one-off sales.
truth: Sod farming for landscaping supply is a real, established agricultural business, and the per-acre economics are cited from a named University Extension source, giving genuine third-party grounding. This is capital- and land-intensive with a long ramp time, which the video is upfront about.

name: Specializing as a plumber in commercial kitchen maintenance for restaurants
cost: Moderate (existing plumbing licensing required)
what: Take the existing plumbing trade and specialize exclusively in commercial kitchen maintenance for restaurants, combining regular maintenance contracts with emergency service, positioning as the go-to specialist for an urgent-need niche (restaurants can't wait days for a kitchen pipe repair) rather than remaining a general residential/commercial plumber.
pitch: The presenter cites a plumber in Perth who built a seven-figure business by focusing exclusively on commercial kitchen maintenance, arguing that becoming irreplaceable to one specific urgent-need client type lets you stop competing on price entirely.
best: Someone already licensed as a plumber (or willing to become one) who wants to niche down into restaurant-specific commercial work rather than general plumbing.
truth: Niche specialization within an established trade, particularly around urgent-need clients like restaurants, is a real, sound business strategy reflected across many trade businesses, and combining maintenance contracts with emergency service is standard practice for building recurring trade-business revenue. Plumbing licensing is a real, non-trivial barrier not detailed here, and the seven-figure example is one presenter-cited case.

name: Mini cheesecakes-in-jars dessert business
cost: Low to moderate startup cost (jars, liners, mixers, an oven or no-bake recipes, refrigeration, labels, and tamper seals)
what: Produce portable, individually-jarred mini cheesecakes (classic, strawberry, chocolate, salted caramel, plus seasonal flavors) for sale as singles or four-packs, with corporate and wedding customization available via lid labels, sold at farmers markets, coffee shops, and via Instagram pre-orders.
pitch: Focus on creamy texture, fresh toppings, and visually appealing layering, using insulated carriers for local delivery and behind-the-scenes baking content to build a following; rotating limited flavors is suggested to keep demand high and encourage repeat purchases rather than a single static menu.
best: Someone comfortable with food production and refrigerated-product logistics (proper cold storage and transport), interested in both retail market sales and event/corporate catering orders.
truth: Jarred, portioned desserts are a well-established, popular format at markets and events because they're easy to sample and transport, and the wedding/corporate customization angle is a credible way to land higher-value orders. This is a perishable, refrigeration-dependent product, so cold-chain logistics and any local cottage-food/health regulations need real attention before scaling beyond a hobby volume.

name: AI-written ebooks self-published through Google Play Books
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Self-publishing AI-written ebooks through Google Play Books' partner program, using ChatGPT to research a trending topic and write the full book, then promoting the listing with an AI-generated SEO blog post.
pitch: The presenter argues Google Play Books is a less-saturated alternative to Amazon KDP with a large built-in audience, and walks through the mechanics: register as a self-published author, find a trending topic via Google Trends, use a pre-built ChatGPT tool to generate a full outline and chapter-by-chapter content, add a disclosure that the book was AI-created, design a cover with ChatGPT, publish, keeping 70% of revenue per the presenter, then generate a promotional blog post via an SEO-writing tool and post it to a free platform linking back to the book.
best: Someone willing to test a less-common publishing platform outside the more crowded Amazon KDP space, and comfortable with the extra promotional step of writing and posting a supporting blog article.
truth: The video's own headline claim, $960 a day from 20 minutes of work, is never substantiated anywhere in the video itself, no earnings screenshot, no account view, no sales data of any kind is shown, a notably weaker evidence standard than most other entries in this database and worth treating with real skepticism. The underlying mechanics described, Google Play Books self-publishing and AI-assisted writing, are real and verifiable independent of that headline number.

name: Reaction/commentary content monetized through Facebook's creator payouts
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Once a Facebook page crosses roughly 4,000 followers, Meta pays creators directly for views on reels, photos, and even stories, unlike Instagram, which generally doesn't pay for organic reach. The specific content strategy discussed is to find already-viral content in a chosen niche (money-making and side-hustle content, in the cited example), play the original clip in the background using a green-screen-style overlay, and record yourself reacting to and adding your own commentary and ideas on top of it, rather than silently pointing at the video.
pitch: The strategy is attributed to a named creator (Chris Corner) reportedly earning around $35,000 a month using this exact method, cranking out five to six of these reaction videos a day across niches once a winning format is found. The presenters note real, checkable audience-behavior context for why this works: Facebook's audience skews older and consumes far more content than it creates, while a lot of Instagram content already auto-posts to a linked Facebook page and quietly picks up far more views there than on Instagram itself, an underused distribution gap.
best: Someone comfortable being on camera for quick reaction-style commentary and willing to post multiple times a day, since the model depends on volume and finding already-proven viral source material rather than one polished video at a time.
truth: This entry is unusually well-sourced on its own limits: one of the presenters shows their own actual, real Facebook monetization earnings live on screen, a modest $4.68 total for the year from a largely inactive page, a genuinely transparent contrast to the $35,000-a-month claim, which is attributed secondhand to another creator's video and not independently verified. The presenters also flag a real platform risk: reposting content and talking about exactly how much money a platform's payout program earns has reportedly gotten some creators' accounts restricted or banned, worth knowing before building a strategy entirely around one platform's creator-payment program.

name: Rank-and-rent local SEO in the AI search era
cost: Very low startup cost (~$25/month per site in tools)
found: AI Rabbit Holes with Ryan Doser (guest: Kyle, the website landlord)
what: The rank-and-rent local SEO business model, ranking simple niche-and-city websites on Google and renting the resulting lead flow to a local business, examined specifically for whether it survives the shift toward AI-generated search answers (Google's AI Overview, AI Mode, and chatbot-based search from tools like ChatGPT and Claude), plus using AI coding tools to build and publish new rank-and-rent sites in minutes instead of days.
pitch: Kyle argues AI has so far only helped the model rather than threatened it, since Google's AI Overview pulls its answers from the same standard search results his sites already rank in, meaning the same 30-year-old ranking fundamentals (clear, locally-specific content and trustworthy backlinks) still determine who gets surfaced, whether by a human scrolling or an AI summarizing. He also notes a practical production shift: content that used to cost him $25 per 500 words and take a freelance writer 10 days now takes seconds with detailed AI prompting, and he's begun building entire rank-and-rent sites in minutes using Claude-based coding tools.
best: Someone with some rank-and-rent or local SEO experience wondering whether the underlying model still holds up as AI search grows, rather than a complete beginner (the core how-to mechanics of picking niches, cities, and doing competitor research are the subject of other, more detailed source material).
truth: Kyle's central claim, that AI search still defers to traditional ranking signals rather than replacing them, is a reasoned argument based on how these systems currently retrieve information, not an independently audited study, and it's a claim that could shift as AI search products continue to change. This underlying rank-and-rent business model itself shows up repeatedly across WAH creator content from multiple practitioners; this interview's distinct contribution is specifically the AI-search-durability question and the AI-accelerated site-building workflow, not the base mechanics of the model.

name: Cloning competitors' winning UGC ads with synthetic AI avatars
cost: Low startup cost (ad-spy and AI avatar tool subscriptions)
what: For an e-commerce or dropshipping store, use an ad-intelligence tool to find competitors' best-performing "ugly," organic-looking UGC video ads (the kind that mimic a real person's unscripted testimonial), then recreate those exact ads almost word-for-word using an AI-generated synthetic avatar reading the same script, swapping details like the model's apparent ethnicity to better match a specific target audience.
pitch: The reasoning is that low-polish, testimonial-style ads (a person seemingly talking to a friend rather than reading a script) consistently outperform studio-quality ads because viewers have become desensitized to obviously polished advertising. The workflow shown is specific: filter an ad-spy tool to competitor ads that have been actively running for 10-plus days (a proxy for "this is working, since nobody keeps paying for an ad that isn't converting"), feed the winning ad's script and the seller's own product details into an AI system to generate a matching prompt, then use an AI avatar-generation tool to produce a synthetic "person" delivering that same script on camera.
best: Someone comfortable operating in a legal and ethical gray area around advertising disclosure, since this is a genuinely powerful technical workflow, but one that raises real questions worth thinking through before using it.
truth: This is worth a direct, upfront caution beyond the usual sourcing caveats: the technique as described is built around closely replicating a specific competitor's existing ad, script and all, and presenting a fabricated AI "person" as though they are a real customer sharing a genuine personal experience with the product, without disclosing that the testimonial is synthetic. That combination, imitating another business's specific creative work and presenting a fabricated persona as an authentic customer story, raises real intellectual-property and truth-in-advertising concerns that go beyond a normal "AI tools speed up ad creation" pitch. The underlying idea of using AI tools to produce UGC-style ads for a store is a legitimate, widely used technique on its own; it's specifically the exact-cloning-plus-fake-testimonial approach described here that deserves real scrutiny before using it.

name: Turning proven Etsy PDF products into interactive mini web apps
cost: Low startup cost (AI coding tool plus an Etsy research tool subscription)
what: Use an Etsy sales-data research tool (the video uses Profit Tree specifically) to find static digital products, spreadsheets, and PDFs already generating real, verifiable sales in a given niche (dating trackers, cleaning planners, mood trackers, fitness challenge trackers, Bible verse reminders), then rebuild the same underlying concept as an interactive mini web app using AI coding tools like Claude Code or Lovable, charging significantly more than the original static version because a working tool has higher perceived value than a document.
pitch: The core argument is that a static spreadsheet or PDF requires real manual effort to use (the video's example: a dating tracker spreadsheet nobody actually fills out consistently), while the same concept as an app that logs an entry in seconds and gives automatic insights removes that friction entirely, justifying a price 5 to 10 times higher. Several specific, checkable proof points from the research tool are cited: a mood-tracker PDF that generated $20,000 on Etsy, a cleaning-planner PDF that generated $100,000, and a Bible-verse PDF product that generated $100,000, each treated as evidence of real demand worth upgrading rather than a product idea invented from scratch.
best: Someone comfortable directing AI coding tools through a multi-step build (describing the app, testing it, giving specific feedback to fix or adjust it) who wants to validate demand using existing sales data before building anything.
truth: The presenter is reasonably transparent about scale, citing a real but modest result (a client's first app made $800 in its first few weeks) rather than only a hypothetical projection, and explicitly cautions against building low-effort "AI slop" apps, framing genuine usefulness as the actual requirement, a fair caveat given how easy these tools make it to generate something superficial. The Etsy sales figures come from a paid third-party research tool's estimates rather than sellers' own confirmed revenue, so they should be treated as directionally useful rather than exact. The video ends promoting the presenter's own upcoming paid community, a financial incentive worth knowing, though the core research-then-build method doesn't require it.

name: AI phone voice assistant for real estate listing calls
cost: Low startup cost
what: Set up an AI voice assistant that answers every incoming phone call for a real estate agent's active listings, 24/7, qualifying buyers, answering property questions, and booking showings directly into the agent's calendar, then charge the agent a flat monthly fee to keep it running.
pitch: The core argument is about missed-call math: a lead that calls at 9pm on a Saturday and gets no answer goes to the next agent who does pick up, and with an average US home commission of $10,000 to $15,000, helping an agent close even one extra deal pays for a $297-$997 monthly fee many times over. The suggested client-sourcing method is free: Zillow's own "find an agent" directory lists active agents with contact info, recent sales volume, and reviews, letting you build a prospect list without any paid tools, then send a short personalized video pitch offering a free 7-day trial built around one of their actual current listings.
best: Someone comfortable with cold outreach (even low-friction video-based outreach) and setting up voice AI software, who wants a recurring-fee service business rather than a one-time project.
truth: The demo call included in the source video is a real, played-back example showing the AI handling specific questions (HOA fees, bedroom count, property taxes) and booking a showing, which is a stronger transparency signal than just describing the capability. This uses a phone/voice channel specifically, distinct from the free-website-plus-chat-widget approach some other creators use to pitch a similar underlying problem (agents losing leads) to the same real estate audience, worth knowing if you're comparing several similar-sounding local-service AI pitches. The specific monthly fee figures ($297 to $997) are the presenter's suggested range, not a benchmark drawn from many real agents' actual willingness to pay.

name: Go-to-market engineering: building AI-powered sales pipelines for other businesses
cost: Low to moderate startup cost (multiple tool subscriptions)
what: Offer businesses a connected system of AI-powered sales tools rather than a single service: finding and qualifying prospects, researching them, drafting personalized outreach, and updating a CRM automatically, effectively building and running a company's outbound sales pipeline as a service rather than doing the selling yourself.
pitch: The presenter frames this as a genuinely new job category (the specific title "go-to-market engineer" is described as barely two years old) with real market pull: a cited agency example (Cold IQ) generating $7 million a year doing exactly this, and job listings in the space paying $150,000 to $250,000 a year for the skill. The suggested 90-day path is concrete and tool-specific: start with basic outbound tooling (a prospect-finding tool, an email or LinkedIn outreach tool), then in month two add an AI-native CRM and an AI note-taker, practicing on small and medium businesses before taking on larger, more complex clients.
best: Someone comfortable connecting several different software tools into one working system (rather than mastering just one), who's interested in the sales and revenue-operations side of a business rather than actually closing deals.
truth: The $7-million agency figure and the cited salary range are presented as real but unverified claims, typical of this kind of overview video, though the general trend, businesses paying well for connected AI-assisted sales tooling, is consistent with similar demand described elsewhere in this database for AI automation and lead-generation services. This does require learning and maintaining several different tools together rather than one simple service, worth knowing before committing to it as a starting point.

name: Simple utility tool websites monetized with display ads
cost: Low startup cost
what: Build simple, single-purpose utility web tools (a word unscrambler, a calculator, a generator) using a no-code AI website builder, then monetize purely through Google AdSense display ads, which pay based on page views shown, not clicks. The video demonstrates building a working word-unscrambler clone from scratch, in plain English prompts, in about 15 minutes.
pitch: The pitch leans on real, checkable examples of this model at scale: a word-unscrambler site pulling an estimated 10-11 million monthly visitors (via the free SimilarWeb Chrome extension) and, at a plausible $9 RPM (earnings per 1,000 page views), roughly $495,000 a month in pure ad revenue. Unlike content businesses that require constant new output, a utility tool solves one evergreen problem and, once built and ranked, keeps running with essentially no maintenance. The suggested research method is specific and checkable: use a keyword tool to find low-competition search terms, then check whether Google is already ranking new, low-trust-score sites for that term, since that's a signal the established competition isn't fully answering the query yet.
best: Someone comfortable with basic SEO research and willing to build and rank multiple small tools (the video recommends a portfolio approach, since any single tool's earnings are unpredictable) rather than betting everything on one site.
truth: The RPM-based revenue estimate for the example site is a calculation from public traffic data and a typical ad-rate range, not a confirmed number from the site's own analytics, so treat the $495,000-a-month figure as illustrative math rather than a verified result. The video is a direct demonstration of, and funnel toward, a specific paid AI website-building tool the presenter promotes throughout (including a referral-commission program for that same tool), a real financial incentive, though the underlying utility-site-plus-AdSense model doesn't require that specific tool to work. Update: a later, more skeptical source video directly examining this genre made a strong, specific case worth weighing seriously. It pointed out that this exact "boring website earns millions, here's how to clone it" video format has been recycled by many different creators with near-identical titles and thumbnails, and that in every version examined, the tutorial itself doubled as an affiliate funnel for a specific paid hosting/website-building tool, meaning the video's real, reliable income is the presenter's affiliate commission, not the cloned utility site's ad revenue. It also raised a concrete, checkable objection to the core pitch: Google ranks new sites partly on domain trust and authority built over years, so a newly published calculator or generator is competing against established, trusted sites (often themselves attached to a bank, a well-known blog, or another authoritative source) for the same search terms, making it genuinely difficult, not simply a matter of building the tool, to ever rank well enough to get meaningful traffic. Its suggested alternative: build a narrow, specific tool for one real paying business client who already needs it, rather than a generic public tool competing for broad search traffic. Worth reading both perspectives before starting: the underlying model can work, but the ranking difficulty and the affiliate-funnel structure behind many of these tutorials are real, specific caveats, not just generic skepticism.

name: Freelance data entry, repositioned as a virtual assistant business
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Start with a simple, accessible skill (data entry) but position yourself to clients as a virtual assistant offering a broader menu of "data entry adjacent" tasks (email and calendar management, customer support, invoicing, Canva design, social media scheduling, creating SOPs), sold as recurring monthly hour packages rather than one-off gigs, so a client is paying for ongoing help rather than a single project.
pitch: The presenter argues that positioning as a data entry specialist specifically limits your client pool, while positioning as a virtual assistant, even with the same underlying skill set, opens up far more small business owners who need broader ongoing help. A concrete pricing example is given: a student named Jessica built three tiered monthly packages (10, 15, and 20 hours a month) starting at $40/hour, so her lowest tier alone was $400 a month recurring for one client. The suggested growth path is to eventually raise your own rate, then hire team members at a lower rate to actually deliver the work, turning the business into a small agency with a much higher ceiling than trading your own hours.
best: Someone comfortable with basic administrative tasks and organized enough to juggle several small recurring clients, who's willing to actively pitch personal networks and small business owners rather than waiting for job board postings.
truth: The tiered recurring-package structure and the specific example given (a real dollar figure tied to a real number of hours) is concrete and checkable math, a good sign, though it's one student's account rather than an audited result. The presenter is upfront that generic entry-level data entry postings on marketplaces like Upwork tend to pay poorly, and recommends the VA positioning specifically as the way around that, a reasonably candid acknowledgment of the entry-level market's real limits. The video promotes the presenter's own paid 90-day accelerator program, a financial incentive worth knowing, though the core positioning and pricing strategy doesn't require it to apply.

name: AI-automated dropshipping: store build, ad-creative cloning, and profit tracking
cost: Very low startup cost (Shopify store and AI tool subscriptions, plus a small ad-testing budget)
what: A from-scratch dropshipping build using AI tools at every stage: Claude analyzes competitor stores and a product image to generate section-by-section copy and branding prompts, which get pasted straight into Shopify's AI store builder to produce a fully branded store in an afternoon. For ad creative, a tool called ECom Boss takes an already-winning ad found organically on TikTok and a product photo, then generates an original ad in that same proven style, skipping the cost of filming or hiring an editor. A separate app, True Profit, automatically pulls product cost, shipping, transaction fees, and ad spend into one dashboard showing true net profit margin rather than just revenue, and supports asking an AI assistant questions about the store's live numbers.
pitch: The presenter frames this as proof that AI has removed the traditional labor bottlenecks in 'lazy dropshipping' — store build, copywriting, and ad creative — leaving only the judgment calls (which ads to scale, which to cut) as the actual work. In a live test, a $50/day ad budget produced 4 orders and $119 in revenue over one weekend, with profit margins holding above 60% after all costs, tracked automatically rather than by hand.
best: Someone comfortable running paid ads and willing to actively manage budget and creative decisions daily, using AI to remove the production bottlenecks (store build, copywriting, ad creative) rather than the decision-making itself.
truth: The one-weekend test shown ($119 revenue, 4 orders) is a genuinely small, real, unembellished result — a plus for honesty — but the video also references a separate, unverified claim of turning that same $50 test into '$50,000 in 45 days' via a different video not shown here, which should be treated as a promotional teaser rather than a demonstrated result. The ad-creative tool is promoted with an affiliate discount code in the video, a financial relationship worth knowing about when weighing the recommendation.

name: A judgment-first Amazon KDP nonfiction publishing framework for an AI-saturated market
cost: Very low startup cost
what: A strategic framework for Amazon KDP nonfiction publishing in an AI-saturated market, combining higher nonfiction pricing with a multi-book portfolio approach rather than betting on one title.
pitch: The presenter, with 12 years in KDP publishing, argues that because AI now lets anyone produce an average book quickly, the real opportunity has shifted from execution to judgment: picking the right niche and buyer, refusing to let AI make every creative decision, and treating a book's cover, title, and positioning as the primary sales lever since Amazon shoppers can't browse a book's interior before buying the way they could in a physical bookstore. He also covers Amazon's AI-disclosure questionnaire during KDP publishing and states that disclosing AI use honestly hasn't hurt his own sales.
best: Someone willing to treat this as a real ongoing publishing business with multiple books and portfolio thinking rather than a single quick project, and comfortable pricing nonfiction higher rather than competing purely on price.
truth: The presenter's core numbers, including $1.2 million in personal book sales and students earning $5,000 to $10,000 a month, are self-reported without account verification shown on screen. He is explicit that a typical individual book in his own portfolio earns closer to $800 to $1,000 a month, with a small fraction of a multi-book portfolio responsible for most of the income, a more grounded and specific framing than a single flashy headline number. The video promotes the presenter's own paid masterclass, mentorship, and done-for-you publishing programs throughout.

name: SaaS discovery-call-first roadmap: zero to 1,000 paying users
cost: Varies (mostly time; low direct cost to start)
what: A general roadmap, not a single product idea, for validating and launching a SaaS product: commit to at least 50 discovery calls before writing any code, only accept real prepayment as validation (not verbal interest), build the smallest possible manual version of the product first, then grow using what Robinson calls the "magic triangle" of LinkedIn content, targeted cold outreach, and retargeting ads working together.
pitch: Robinson, who's built three software companies to a combined $35 million in ARR, is specific about the mechanics at each stage: ask prospects six exact questions on discovery calls (including "I'm thinking of charging X per month, would you pay that price?"), do everything manually before automating (his company RB2B sent leads via spreadsheet email for five months before building a website), and look for three concrete product-market-fit signals, weekly referrals, customers who'd be upset to lose it, and organic growth with zero marketing, before investing in scale.
best: Someone willing to do real, unscalable manual outreach and service delivery early on rather than jumping straight to automation, and comfortable posting consistently and personally on LinkedIn as part of the growth strategy.
truth: Robinson discloses he built and is promoting his own product, RB2B (a website-visitor identification tool), as part of the outreach and retargeting strategy he describes, worth knowing since parts of the roadmap are shaped around that tool's specific use case. The discovery-call questions, manual-first building philosophy, and specific product-market-fit signals are general, independently useful advice regardless of which tools you choose to execute the growth engine with.

name: AI-assisted, evidence-based Amazon affiliate content across blog, Pinterest, and YouTube
cost: Low startup cost (time, and ideally owning or borrowing the products reviewed)
found: Affiliate marketing / AI content YouTube creator
what: Building affiliate content, including blog reviews, Pinterest pins, and YouTube videos, around real hands-on product evidence such as original photos, a stated testing methodology, and first-hand notes, then using AI only to organize and speed up the writing, and distributing the same core research across Google, Pinterest's Amazon-linking feature, and YouTube.
pitch: The presenter argues the old thin-content, keyword-first affiliate playbook is losing to AI-generated competition, so the differentiator now is genuine hands-on evidence that AI can format but can't invent. He walks through a specific 30-day plan: pick a narrow product cluster and gather evidence in week one, publish one piece of proof content in week two, build a 12-pin Pinterest layer in week three, and expand the cluster with more content in week four.
best: Someone willing to actually acquire and test physical products, whether by buying, borrowing, or otherwise getting hands-on access, rather than someone hoping to run this purely by prompting AI with no product access.
truth: The presenter repeats more than once that AI can transform your evidence but can't be the evidence, a notably candid caveat compared to some other AI-content pitches, since it directly warns against the shortcut version of this same idea. No personal income figures are given for the presenter's own results with this specific method; effectiveness is illustrated through other established channels' examples rather than the presenter's own numbers, so it's unclear how quickly a new creator could expect traction.

name: Multi-network affiliate marketing with a nurture funnel
cost: Very low startup cost
what: Rather than creating your own product, become a skilled marketer for other people's digital products (courses, ebooks, software), sourced from affiliate networks like Digistore24, ClickBank, and WarriorPlus, earning a 50-80% commission per sale. Instead of dropping a raw affiliate link, build a simple funnel: an opt-in landing page collecting an email address, followed by a multi-day "nurture sequence" of short, genuinely useful content on the topic that builds trust before ever presenting the affiliate offer.
pitch: The core argument is that affiliate marketing removes the hardest, slowest parts of building a product-based business (six to twelve months of product development, pricing, merchant accounts, sales pages) since the product already exists and is already priced and tested. The presenter frames the funnel-and-nurture-sequence structure as the actual differentiator over just posting a bare affiliate link, since people buy from someone they've gotten to know and trust over several days of free value, not from a stranger's link. Traffic is driven through free organic short-form content (Instagram and TikTok, posting one to three videos a day), tracking which specific formats perform well and repeating those rather than constantly inventing new ones.
best: Someone comfortable being consistently on camera or creating short-form content, and willing to build out a funnel and email sequence rather than just posting links, since that infrastructure is described as the actual differentiator here.
truth: The presenter is specific that commissions from these networks can be high (a cited $3,363 product paying an 80% commission), and that these are checkable, real figures visible on the platforms themselves, a good transparency signal. The claimed $25,000 to $30,000 monthly income and the $3 million lifetime figure are personal claims without independent verification, and the video ends by promoting a free masterclass, a funnel of its own worth being aware of, separate from whether the core affiliate-plus-funnel mechanic works.

name: Medical student coaching business
cost: Low startup cost
found: Alex Hormozi interviewing a vascular surgery resident
what: A coaching business aimed at medical students, built and run by a doctor while he was still in medical and surgical training, requiring roughly an hour a day of his time and reaching about $500,000 a year in revenue and roughly $400,000 a year in profit over five years.
pitch: Hormozi highlights this as a case of someone about to start a high-paying surgical career who instead already has a coaching business generating comparable income for a small fraction of the working hours, and argues the coaching business has a much higher ceiling to scale further than trading additional hours for surgical pay does.
